In Genesis and the Kings, it primarily designates the officers of the kings of Egypt and Israel: Potiphar (Genesis 37:36, 39:1), the officers of Pharaoh (Genesis 40:2, 40:7), the servants of the king of Israel (1 Samuel 8:15, 1 Kings 22:9). The book of Esther makes extensive use of it to speak of the servants of the court of King Ahasuerus, responsible for the management and guarding of the threshold (Esther 1:10, 2:3, 2:21). In Isaiah, the prophet addresses the eunuch as a symbol of one who believes he is excluded from the divine covenant (Isaiah 56:3-4). Daniel uses the word to designate the chief of the servants of the king of Babylon who must educate the young Jewish captives (Daniel 1:3 to 1:18). The meaning nuances: sometimes the word designates a castrated servant, sometimes a simple high-ranking officer, but always under the dependency of a king.
H5631.portee: The word eunuch invites the reader to contemplate God's mercy towards those who seem rejected or diminished. Isaiah promises the eunuch, a figure of one who believes he is separated from the people of God, that he will have a place and a name in the house of the Lord (Isaiah 56:3-5): a radical word of consolation. It is a call to see beyond appearances and human conditions to recognize the dignity that God confers to each person, even to the one who seems most excluded.

sens: Person who exercises authority over others in administration
One who directs and supervises a function or area
Responsible person accountable to higher authority
H5632.detail:
1. The word designates a person vested with administrative authority. In the context of Daniel, the king entrusts the governance of the kingdom to three chiefs who supervise the satraps (Daniel 6:2). It is an official and visible charge, often related to state management.

2. The chief is responsible for specific areas and must account for them. Daniel "surpassed the chiefs and the satraps" by his excellence and integrity (Daniel 6:3): he fulfilled his mission faithfully. The word does not designate a slave or a subordinate without power, but someone in a position of direction.

3. Chiefs often form a college or group of authority that acts together to govern. In Daniel 6:7, "all the chiefs of the kingdom" are consulted for major decisions. It is therefore also a hierarchical administrative function, below the king but above simple executors.
H5632.origine: The Hebrew word סָרֵךְ (sarekh) is probably related to Persian administration, reflecting the historical context of the book of Daniel, written during the Babylonian exile. It designates a "supervisor" or "master," someone who orders and controls. The root evokes the idea of leading a line, a sequence of people.
H5632.emploi: The word appears 5 times, all in Daniel 6, during the account of Daniel being appointed chief by King Darius. These chiefs are responsible for royal administration, tasked with supervising the satraps (provincial officials). They collaborate with the king to govern, but also become jealous adversaries of Daniel, seeking an accusation against him (6:4, 6:6). The use of the word emphasizes formal authority and the ability to harm if misused: the chiefs attempt to manipulate the king to eliminate a rival. The Persian historical context strongly marks this administrative vocabulary.
H5632.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible recognizes legitimate power and authority, even in pagan governments. For the reader, it is an invitation to serve with integrity "in one's charge," as Daniel did: without unjustified fear, without compromise, remaining faithful to one's convictions even under pressure. Daniel's example shows that moral excellence is more powerful than jealous machinations.

sens: Sovereign or political leader of a region
One who exercises power and gives orders
Person of high rank, vested with authority
H5633A.detail:
1. The word designates a sovereign or leader who governs a region and bears the title of power. In the Old Testament, it mainly applies to the five princes of the Philistines, each at the head of a city: the prince of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron (Joshua 13:3). These are recognized local authorities.

2. It is one who commands and decides. The princes of the Philistines gather the other leaders, consult them, and execute decisions (Judges 16:27: "all the princes of the Philistines were there"). They have the power to call people to war or to negotiate with enemies (1 Samuel 29:6).

3. The word carries a dignity, a high social rank. A prince is an important man, regarded with respect or fear. He is not a mere village chief, but a true master: in the narratives, he is implicitly opposed to the ordinary people.
H5633A.origine: The Hebrew word סֶרֶן (sèren) has an obscure root, but it is related to forms that evoke command and authority in closely related Semitic languages. It is used in the Bible only for the Philistine leaders, making it a specialized term to designate this category of foreign rulers. The concentration of the word on the Philistines suggests that the biblical writers wanted to designate these enemies with a title that marked their distinct political power.
H5633A.emploi: The word appears 19 times, almost exclusively in narratives featuring the Philistines and Samson (Judges 16, 1 Samuel 5-7, 29). It always designates one of the five supreme authorities of the major Philistine cities: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. In these texts, the princes act together or individually: they consult a diviner together to find out how to stop Samson (Judges 16:23), they gather for the spectacle of his downfall (Judges 16:27), they receive military advice (1 Samuel 29:6-7). The word always describes a position of executive power and prestige, never of mere soldiers or officials. It is an official title, a function of territorial governance.
H5633A.portee: This word reminds the reader that God recognizes and judges the political powers of the world, even if they are pagan and foreign. The Philistine princes are not insignificant figures: they are authority figures with civil and military responsibilities. It also shows that the Bible does not view power as absolute: Samson, enslaved by the Philistines, brings down the house where the princes gather, illustrating how God can break human order and its power structures for the benefit of His people.

sens: metal rod that passes through a wheel to make it turn
articulated support of a wheel on a vehicle
H5633B.detail:
1. The axle is the metal piece (usually made of brass, that is, bronze) that passes through the center of a wheel and allows it to turn. It is the axis around which the wheel pivots. In Solomon's temple, the bases that were rolled for the rituals had wheels of brass mounted on brass axles (1 Kings 7:30).
2. By extension, it is the support that connects the wheels to the structure of the vehicle or mobile object. The axles allow the weight to rest on the wheels and enable the vehicle to move.
H5633B.origine: The Hebrew word סֶרֶן (seren) specifically refers to this mechanical part of a wheel. It is a technical term related to carts and wheeled vehicles, known in the ancient Near Eastern world. The word belongs to the vocabulary of metalworking and machine construction.
H5633B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 7:30, where it describes the brass axles of the rolling bases of Solomon's temple. These bases were mobile structures used for storing or moving elements of sacred furniture. The technical usage and rarity of the word reflect the sophistication of metalworking during the royal period.
H5633B.portee: This word reminds us of the beauty and complexity of Solomon's temple, built with precious materials and remarkable craftsmanship. It invites meditation on the care given to the house of God, even in the most functional details.

sens: woody offshoot that detaches from the trunk or main branch of a tree
by extension, the leafy or productive part of a tree
H5634.detail:
1. A branch is the woody part that grows on the trunk of a tree and divides itself into smaller twigs. It is the structure through which the tree expands and broadens. In Ezekiel 31:5, the branches of the great cedar that extend symbolize its power and dominance over all surrounding trees.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the entire foliage and twigs of a branch, that is, the living and productive part of the tree: this is where leaves, flowers, and fruits are born.
H5634.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of division or separation: the branch separates from the trunk. The same concept is found in other Hebrew words that denote divisions and ramifications. This term precisely describes the natural and visible structure of the tree.
H5634.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 31:5. It is part of a prophetic vision where the prophet describes a great cedar whose branches multiply and extend due to the abundance of water. In this context, the branches symbolize growth, strength, and the radiance of a powerful rule. The cedar and its branches represent an empire or a king in the glory of its dominion.
H5634.portee: This passage invites the reader to contemplate the greatness of creation: how a tree, nourished by water, spreads its branches to cover and dominate all that surrounds it. It is also an image of earthly power, useful for understanding how the Bible speaks of empires and their temporal glory, which can be shattered by God's judgment.

sens: Consume by fire
Cremate a dead body
H5635.detail:
1. To consume by fire: this is the action of reducing something to ashes by flame. The word evokes complete and irreversible destruction by fire.
2. To cremate a dead body: in Amos 6:10, the context of plague or catastrophe leads a relative to burn the remains of a dead person, probably for hygiene reasons or funeral ritual in circumstances of extreme urgency. This is a rare and exceptional practice in Israel, contrasting with the usual burial.
H5635.origine: The verb belongs to the family of the word שָׂרַף (saraph), which fundamentally means "to burn" or "to consume." The present form (Pael) intensifies the action: "to make burn," "to burn completely." The same verb also designates the seraphim (שְׂרָפִים), the "fiery beings" or "burning ones" of Isaiah's vision, named perhaps for their brilliance or their nature of spiritual fire.
H5635.emploi: This verb appears only once at this point in the preserved biblical text (Amos 6:10). It describes an exceptional funeral act: during an epidemic or calamity, a survivor burns the bones of a dead person to cremate them, instead of burying them according to the usual Israelite custom. This unique usage reflects a situation of extreme distress where normal rites cannot be observed.
H5635.portee: This passage reminds the believer that calamities and judgments from God can be so terrible that they disrupt even the most sacred religious practices. It calls for taking the prophet's warning seriously and not relying on divine protection when one strays away from it.

sens: A spiny desert plant, wild and invasive
A weed that symbolizes barrenness and desolation
H5636.detail:
1. The thornbush is a desert plant that grows naturally, covered with sharp thorns: it is a hostile and sterile vegetation, typical of arid and abandoned lands. In Isaiah 55:13, God promises that where the thornbush grows, the cypress will rise in its place — the image is one of radical transformation, from the barren to the beautiful and useful.
2. Figuratively, the thornbush represents the absence of blessing and the state of ruin: a land covered with thornbushes is a land that man has neglected or that God has abandoned to desolation. Its replacement by the myrtle in the divine promise symbolizes the return to abundance and life.
H5636.origine: The Hebrew word is rare and its exact meaning remains uncertain: it probably refers to a spiny desert plant, perhaps a thornbush or a variety of thistle. Its image evokes sterility and abandonment, in contrast to cultivated plants and fruit trees that symbolize blessing.
H5636.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 55:13, in an oracle of restoration and joy. God's promise transforms the sterile desert: in place of useless thorny plants, noble and productive trees will arise. This passage marks the transition from curse to blessing, from chaos to divine order.
H5636.portee: This biblical image invites the believer to contemplate the transformative power of God: what seems lost, barren, or hostile to life can be completely transfigured by divine grace. It teaches hope: the Lord does not leave His children in ruin, but promises restoration and beauty beyond present desolation.

sens: Refusing to obey, revolting against authority
Having an untamable character, not allowing oneself to be controlled
Persisting in disobedience despite warnings
Resisting God and His commandments
H5637.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the act of refusing to obey a legitimate authority: a son who does not listen "neither to the voice of his father nor to the voice of his mother" (Deuteronomy 21:18), leaders who act against established justice (Isaiah 1:23).
2. It then characterizes an untamable temperament, someone who cannot be bent: like a stubborn horse that refuses the yoke, or a sheep that "softens" against its will, the rebellious one does not submit naturally (Hosea 4:16).
3. The word often emphasizes persistence: rebellion does not cease despite corrections or calls to return (Nehemiah 9:29: "they persisted in their pride").
4. Applied to the people of God, it means deliberately rejecting His commandments and His law to follow "a wicked way, according to their thoughts" (Isaiah 65:2). It is a form of spiritual pride: man asserts himself against God Himself.
H5637.origine: The Hebrew verb sarár comes from a root expressing the idea of stiffness, hardness, or that which bands against. It primarily appears in the Qal (simple form), expressing the state or attitude of one who rebels. In the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word is often rendered by apeitheó (to refuse to obey) or similar terms. The word family includes other forms that reinforce this notion of stiffness and insubordination.
H5637.emploi: This verb appears 16 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in the form of an adjective or participle ("the one who rebels"). It is found in the Law (Deuteronomy), the Psalms, the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Zechariah), and in historical texts (Nehemiah). The context varies: sometimes it concerns the rebellion of a son against his parents (Deuteronomy 21:18-20), sometimes corrupt leaders (Isaiah 1:23), and sometimes the entire people refusing to listen to divine law (Nehemiah 9:29, Psalms 78:8). The word always emphasizes not only disobedience but also voluntary hardening, pride that refuses to bend.
H5637.portee: This word reminds us that rebellion is never neutral: it is an active, stubborn refusal to submit to God. It invites the believer to examine their own heart to discern attitudes of spiritual stiffness—hidden refusals, resistances to God's order. It also shows that God is not overcome by this rebellion: it only exacerbates the distance between man and his Creator, and it determines divine judgment.

sens: The cold season of the year, marked by cold and rain
The time of year when vegetation lies dormant and the earth rests
Figuratively, a difficult season, a time of sterility or absence
H5638.detail:
1. Winter is the cold season of the year, when abundant rains fall in Israel. In Song of Solomon 2:11, the poet sings that winter is past and the rain has ceased: it is the return of spring, a symbol of renewal and the life that returns.
2. Winter also represents the season when nature sleeps, when the earth produces nothing. It is a time of waiting and rest, before the fertility of spring and summer returns.
3. Spiritually, winter can evoke a difficult season of life, a time when God seems silent or when blessing is delayed—but the biblical message is that after winter, spring always comes.
H5638.origine: The Hebrew word *sətāv* simply denotes the cold and rainy season, which the Jews referred to as the rainy season. In the Eastern Mediterranean, winter is accompanied by essential rains for agriculture. The word may be related to the idea of "cover" or "shelter," as clouds and rains cover the sky during this season.
H5638.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 2:11. It is a poetic evocation where spring follows winter: the poet celebrates the moment when the rains cease and flowers and birds return. This image of the transition from winter to spring symbolizes the renewal of love and life. The context is clearly one of describing the beauty of nature in spring.
H5638.portee: Winter reminds the reader that seasons change and that difficult times do not last. After winter, spring always returns: it is a message of hope for those going through a season of spiritual dryness or suffering. This verse from the Song invites us to see in the cycles of nature a reflection of God's faithfulness and the renewal He brings to our lives.

sens: A man from the time of the Exodus, a spy sent by Moses
H5639.detail: Sethur is one of the twelve men chosen by Moses to explore the land of Canaan before Israel's entry. He represents the tribe of Asher during this reconnaissance mission. His name means "hidden" in Hebrew, which could evoke the idea of secrecy or discretion suited to his reconnaissance mission.
H5639.origine: The name Sethur carries the meaning "hidden" or "concealed." It is a Hebrew name formed from the root "str" which expresses the idea of hiding, setting aside, or keeping secret. This name and its etymology reflect biblical Hebrew, where proper names often carry symbolic meaning.
H5639.emploi: Sethur appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:13, where he is named among the twelve spies sent to scout the promised land. He is presented as the representative of the tribe of Asher and the son of Michael. This unique mention places Sethur in the foundational narrative of the people of Israel, during the exodus from Egypt and the journey to Canaan.

sens: To close, obstruct an opening or passage
To fill, to fill a void
To keep secret, to keep hidden
To confine, to prevent from escaping
H5640A.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to close or obstruct: to block a water source, a well, a passage. In 2 Chronicles 32:3, King Hezekiah "closes" the water sources to deprive the enemy of this vital resource. It is the physical action of barring, blocking.
2. To fill means to completely fill a void: in Genesis 26:15, the Philistines fill the wells dug by Abraham's servants with dirt. The hole disappears.
3. To keep secret or hidden applies to what one wants to keep from view: in Daniel 8:26, the prophet is instructed to keep a vision "secret." The word emphasizes here a closure of the mouth, a restraint of speech.
4. To penetrate (in Psalms 51:8) is a rarer and figurative use: "Make wisdom penetrate within me"—here the verb evokes rather the idea of making enter, of deeply imprinting in the heart, as one drives something in.
H5640A.origine: The Hebrew verb סָתַם (satam) comes from a root that expresses the idea of closing, blocking, of closure. The word family includes nouns designating what is closed or secret. The basic image is that of obstruction, of physical closure: one blocks a passage to prevent it from functioning. It is a concrete word that has enriched itself with figurative uses, notably to express secrecy (the closed mouth, the restrained word).
H5640A.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in narratives and prophetic texts. The concrete uses (blocking sources, filling wells) regularly appear in the narratives of Hezekiah and the kings (2 Kings, 2 Chronicles): these are military strategies to weaken the enemy. The figurative use in the sense of "secret" or "hidden" appears in prophetic visions (Daniel 8:26, 12:4, 12:9) where it concerns keeping a revelation hidden until its fulfillment. Once (Psalms 51:8), the word takes the meaning of "to penetrate" or "to drive in" in the context of a heartfelt prayer.
H5640A.portee: This word reminds us that God can close or open accesses—to water, to food, to paths. It also evokes the importance of confidentiality in divine revelations: some things must remain hidden until the appointed time. For the believer, it is an invitation to distinguish what should be kept secret (the mysteries of God) from what should be proclaimed. The verb also emphasizes that God's secret is never a mere prohibition, but a protection for a future purpose.

sens: Action of closing, obstructing, blocking access
Assistance provided in need, aid
H5640B.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the concrete action of closing or blocking something to prevent access — like obstructing an opening or passage. In Lamentations 3:8, the prophet cries out to God saying, "He does not allow access to my prayer": the word conveys the idea that the way to God is blocked, closed, inaccessible due to darkness and sorrow.
2. By extension, the word also means "help" or "aid" — it is the action of coming to someone's assistance in distress. This nuance appears when we understand that the prophet cries out for help, asking for a door to be opened, for access to God's mercy to be restored. Help is what liberates access, what restores broken communication.
H5640B.origine: The Hebrew verb sa.tam comes from a root that expresses the idea of closing or blocking. The same family of words describes the act of stopping, obstructing, putting up an obstacle. The underlying image is that of a physical obstruction — something that is sealed or closed to prevent passage. When applied to help, we imagine the reversal of this process: opening what was closed, creating a passage where there was none.
H5640B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Lamentations 3:8, where the prophet Jeremiah, crushed by the misfortunes of Jerusalem, cries out to God but sees his prayer refused. The expression "does not allow access to my prayer" uses this verb to describe the painful experience of a God who seems to have closed the door, blocking the usual access to His grace. It is a moment of extreme distress, where the prophet feels isolated, without recourse. The word captures the emotional intensity: not only does God not respond, but He seems to have sealed the entrance, making any communication impossible.
H5640B.portee: This verse reminds the reader that God's supplications are never definitively ignored, even when there seems to be silence or refusal. Lamentations itself testifies that crying out to God, expressing distress, is already a form of prayer heard. For the Christian facing a sense of distance from God, this passage invites perseverance in prayer and recognition that the God of Israel never permanently closes the door of compassion.

sens: To put something or someone out of sight, to conceal
To withdraw, to evade the sight of others or to put oneself in safety
To turn away one's gaze, to refuse to look
To keep secret, to reserve without revealing
H5641.detail:
1. To hide means to put something out of sight, making it invisible or inaccessible. Cain fears being hidden from the face of God after his murder (Genesis 4:14): he dreads being cast away, separated from divine presence. David hides in strongholds to escape Saul who pursues him (1 Samuel 23:19).
2. To hide is also to voluntarily evade sight, to withdraw to safety to avoid danger or judgment. The prudent man hides when he sees evil coming, while the fool continues and suffers the consequences (Proverbs 27:12).
3. To hide can also mean to turn away one's gaze, to refuse to see or listen. When God hides His face, He turns away His attention, support, or help. This expresses both anger and abandonment (Psalms 10:11; Isaiah 57:17).
4. Finally, to hide means to keep secret, to guard hidden for oneself. In Proverbs 25:2, it is the glory of God to conceal a matter, to reserve it, not to lay it bare before the public.
H5641.origine: The Hebrew verb סָתַר (satar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering, putting a veil over something. In the Hebrew Bible, this verb appears in several forms that nuance the action: hiding oneself, being hidden, hiding carefully. The word shares a family with סֵתֶר (seter), which means "refuge" or "retreat" — a place where one hides, where one is protected. This root expresses both the human act of concealing and the behavior of God who withdraws or hides.
H5641.emploi: This very commonly used verb (80 occurrences) appears throughout the Bible, from the Pentateuch to the prophets. It first describes concrete situations: Cain fears being hidden from God (Genesis 4:14), David hides from persecutors (1 Samuel 23:19), Joash is hidden by his nurse (2 Kings 11:2). But the word also takes on a profound theological dimension: it expresses the relationship between God and man. God hides secrets (Jeremiah 16:17), hides His plans (Isaiah 45:15), or hides His face as a sign of anger or abandonment (Psalms 27:9, 88:15, Isaiah 57:17). The Psalms constantly refer to it to express either divine protection ("hide me under the shadow of Your wings," Psalms 17:8) or the distress of one who feels God withdrawing.
H5641.portee: This word reveals an important truth: God sees everything, even what is hidden from men, and nothing can escape Him (Jeremiah 16:17; 23:24). For the believer, this calls for honesty and sincerity before God. At the same time, hiding is also an act of protection: God hides His children to preserve them from evil (Psalms 27:5), and the wise man hides from danger (Proverbs 27:12). The believer thus learns to distinguish between futile hiding from God and the trust that takes refuge in Him.

sens: to make invisible, to remove from sight
to shelter, to protect
to keep secret, to conceal
H5642A.detail:
1. To hide means to make invisible or to remove something from sight. In Daniel 2:22, God "reveals what is deep and hidden": it refers to hidden mysteries, invisible to the human eye, known only to the Lord.
2. To hide can also mean to shelter or protect, as one hides something in safety. It is the idea of removing from destruction or danger.
3. By extension, to hide means to keep secret or to conceal: to keep for oneself what one does not want others to know. Hidden things are those that are not revealed, that are kept veiled.
H5642A.origine: The Aramaic verb se.tar comes from an ancient Semitic root that originally means "to cover" or "to enclose." It is related to the Hebrew sa.tar (סָתַר), which has the same meaning. This family of words always speaks of something that is covered, enclosed, removed from sight — whether voluntarily or by nature.
H5642A.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:22, within the grand discourse of Nebuchadnezzar recognizing God's wisdom. Here, the word applies to deep and secret things — the mysteries of the past, present, and future — that only God knows and of which He alone can lift the veil. The context is that of divine revelation: God removes the veil from hidden secrets to make them known to the one who worships Him.
H5642A.portee: This verse teaches that nothing escapes God's knowledge: what is hidden from us is manifest to Him. This invites the believer to trust and humility before the Lord, who sees all secrets and cannot be deceived. It is also a promise: God can reveal what was unknown to us, illuminating our spiritual darkness.

sens: To demolish, to reduce a building or structure to ruins
H5642B.detail: 1. To demolish, to reduce a building or structure to ruins — it is to physically annihilate a structure, reducing it to nothing. In Ezra 5:12, this verb describes the action of Nebuchadnezzar who destroys the temple of Jerusalem: the king "destroyed this house," meaning he razed it, dismantling it stone by stone to annihilate it.
H5642B.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a root meaning "to break" or "to shatter." The word belongs to the family of terms that express the physical and definitive destruction of something. In Hebrew and Aramaic, this root evokes the image of an abandoned ruin, a house emptied of its substance.
H5642B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament of the provided biblical corpus, in Ezra 5:12. It is used to describe an act of military and political destruction: that of the temple by a foreign power. The context is that of the Babylonian exile, where the ruin of the sanctuary marks divine judgment on the people's unfaithfulness.
H5642B.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the destruction of the temple was a tangible consequence of the people's turning away from God. It invites reflection on the seriousness of divine warnings and the reality of judgment when the people persist in rebellion. It is also a call to repentance: the temple will be rebuilt, as announced in the continuation of Ezra.

sens: What is hidden, concealed, not visible
Place where one hides, protected shelter
Action of hiding, keeping secret
Character of what is done away from sight
Divine or human protection against danger
Malicious intent that is concealed
H5643A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is covered or hidden — a veil, a physical shelter. In Job 24:15, the adulterer watches for twilight by putting "a veil over his face": he hides so that no one can see him.
2. A secret is also a secluded place where one takes refuge, a location that provides protection. In 1 Samuel 19:2, David is invited to stay "in a secluded place" to be safe from Saul. It is a refuge.
3. The word also refers to the action of keeping something secret, doing something away from sight. In Deuteronomy 13:6, the incitement to idol worship is done "secretly," without a witness.
4. More broadly, it is the state of protection, intimacy with God. In Psalms 31:21, God protects his beloved "under the shelter of his face," meaning in his hidden communion, away from persecutors.
5. Finally, the word can evoke a concealed intention, often evil. In Proverbs 25:23, a "mysterious tongue" (which hides its thoughts) provokes anger.
6. The secret can also be that of God himself: his hidden plans that he reveals only to those he chooses, as in Isaiah 48:16.
H5643A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cover, to close." It is related to the idea of what veils, protects, or conceals. The same root gives rise to words designating a lid, a secret, and more broadly, anything that is hidden from view. In Hebrew, a secret is something intrinsically hidden, protected, separated.
H5643A.emploi: This word appears 35 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets. The Segond translates it as "secret," "secretly," "shelter," "retreat," "asylum," "refuge" depending on the context. In Psalms, the secret is often that of divine refuge (Psalms 27:5; 91:1): the believer finds protection "in the secret" of God. In Proverbs, the secret pertains to intentions, often hidden and evil (Proverbs 25:23). In legislative passages (Deuteronomy 27), the secret refers to concealed acts believed to be unpunished. In the prophets, God reveals or hides his secrets: Isaiah 45:19 states that God does not speak in secret, unlike the mute idols.
H5643A.portee: This word teaches the reader that nothing escapes God, even what is done in secret. It also reminds him that God himself is a refuge, a shelter where the believer finds protection and peace away from persecution. The secret invites trust: knowing the hidden secrets of God is to believe in his hidden plans for our good.

sens: Shelter, refuge where one is covered and safe
Action of covering, putting to safety
Support and defense offered to someone
Help, aid in danger
H5643B.detail: 1. The word first evokes the concrete image of a shelter, a place that covers and protects: like a roof that keeps you safe from rain or sun. 2. It also designates the action of covering someone, putting them in safety against threats: it is the idea of watching over them. 3. From there, it means the support and defense that an authority or power offers to those who depend on it: a king protects his subjects. 4. Lastly, it is the help, the assistance given to someone in distress, as when one intervenes to save them from danger. In Deuteronomy 32:38, Moses ironically questions: have the false gods that the Israelites worshiped ever covered them with this protection, this help that a true god should provide?
H5643B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to hide, to cover." This same root produces other words related to the idea of refuge and hiding place: something that hides and protects. The basic image is that of covering something to put it out of sight and danger.
H5643B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:38. It is found in the Song of Moses, the great poem where Moses reminds the people of all that the God of Israel has done for them. At this specific point, Moses accuses the Israelites of wanting to turn to other gods: he ironically challenges them to show him if these false gods have ever protected, covered, or helped them. The word expresses what a true god must do for his people: cover, defend, help them. It is a divine protection that one should seek, not that of mute idols.
H5643B.portee: This word reminds the believer of a fundamental truth: only God offers true protection. Our modern idols — money, power, reputation — never truly cover us from danger. Divine protection, however, is reliable and complete. The text invites each generation to recognize that our security comes solely from the living God, and to seek in him the refuge that no human or created power can offer.

sens: Levite from the time of Egypt and the desert
H5644.detail: Sithri is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the moment when Moses lists the genealogies of the families of Levi. He is the son of Uzziel, who is himself the son of Kohath (the son of Levi). His brothers are Mishael, Elzaphan, and Ishiah. Although the Bible recounts nothing of his exploits, his name appears in the sacred genealogy of the chosen people, which shows that he has a place in the history of salvation, even if it remains discreet.
H5644.origine: The name Sithri means "protection of Jehovah": it combines the idea of protection or covering with the divine name. This name expresses a family's trust in the protection of the living God during the time of Egyptian slavery. He belongs to the Levitical branch of the Kohathites, those who were responsible for the most sacred objects of the Tabernacle.
H5644.emploi: Sithri appears only once in Scripture, in Exodus 6:22, during the detailed genealogy of the descendants of Levi that Moses reports at the time of the first divine manifestation in the desert. This mention, although brief, places him in the genealogical continuity of Israel and confirms that he lived at the pivotal time between slavery in Egypt and the crossing of the desert. No particular act is attributed to him; his presence in the text is genealogical and not narrative.

sens: A mass of water vapor floating in the sky
Darkness, thick shadow that hides
Manifestation of the divine presence
H5645.detail:
1. The cloud is primarily the visible cloud in the sky: a mass of condensed vapor. This is the most common meaning of the word in Hebrew. At harvest time, one who looks at the uncertain clouds will not bring in their harvest, for they fear bad weather (Ecclesiastes 11:4).

2. The word also refers to darkness, shadow, or that which hides: when God covers the sky with clouds, light disappears beneath the thickness of the clouds. The psalmist sings: "From the splendor that went before Him, clouds poured out" (Psalms 18:13), evoking the power of a storm.

3. In divine revelation, the cloud becomes the visible sign of the presence of the Lord. God says to Moses: "I will come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you" (Exodus 19:9). The cloud both conceals and reveals: it veils the Lord while attesting to His arrival.
H5645.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of fog, darkness, and density. The connection with water and the atmosphere is central: a cloud is literally what fills the air and fills it with shadow. This image of the opaque veil will be taken up in biblical tradition to signify the mysterious proximity of God, who manifests Himself without being fully visible.
H5645.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the poetic (Psalms, Job, Ecclesiastes) and prophetic (Isaiah, Jeremiah) books. In a meteorological sense, it describes natural phenomena: rain comes when clouds gather (1 Kings 18:45), the Lord suspends water in the clouds (Job 26:8). In a theophanic (divine) sense, the cloud marks God's intervention: it accompanies Him when He comes to judge Egypt (Isaiah 19:1), it protects Israel in the desert, it fills the Tabernacle. The word oscillates between the natural and the supernatural, the visible and the hidden.
H5645.portee: For the Christian, the cloud reminds us that God is never far away, but often veiled from our sight. It invites us to respect His mystery and to recognize His signs, even when we do not see Him clearly. It also teaches that faith must persevere in the face of darkness, like Moses who entered the cloud on Mount Sinai to meet the Lord.

sens: Architectural element that projects or stands out
Step or level of a staircase or platform
Horizontal band or frieze that runs along a wall or structure
H5646.detail:
1. This word designates a construction element that protrudes or projects: it is a part of a building's structure that creates relief or depth. In the temple described in the book of Ezekiel, a "wooden entablature" adorns the vestibule (Ezekiel 41:25), forming a sort of decorative band or crown.
2. The word can also refer to a step or level: an elevated surface that one uses to ascend. At the portico of Solomon's temple, there are "steps" that precede the columns (1 Kings 7:6), allowing access to the main structure.
3. In a broader architectural context, it is a frieze or cornice that horizontally adorns a wall, often placed in relief to create an effect of shadow and light.
H5646.origine: The Hebrew word עָב (av) has an uncertain origin, but it belongs to the vocabulary of architects and craftsmen. Its primary meaning refers to a projection, an advance, or an elevation. Although its exact root is debated among specialists, the context of the passages where it appears shows that it is a precise technical term of building, particularly used to describe the ornaments and structural elements of the temple.
H5646.emploi: The word עָב (av) appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in architectural descriptions of the temple. It first appears in 1 Kings 7:6, where it designates the steps of Solomon's temple portico, a practical and visible element. It reappears twice in Ezekiel's vision of the temple (41:25 and 41:26), where it describes more ornamental elements: a wooden band that adorns the vestibule, then other similar details on the side walls. Its usage thus varies between a more utilitarian sense (step) and a more decorative sense (frieze, entablature), but always within a sacred and architectural framework.
H5646.portee: This word reminds us that the temple was not just a functional building, but a structure designed in its smallest details. Each element, down to the smallest ornaments and steps, reflected the greatness and holiness of the God being worshiped. It is an invitation to understand that in the life of faith, attention to detail and beauty glorifies the Lord.

sens: To work for someone, to perform a task under their authority
To be subject, submissive to someone as a subject or inferior
To honor God or a deity through worship and obedience
To be constrained or forced into servitude
H5647G.detail:
1. The word first describes the concrete work done by someone on behalf of another: it is to labor, to execute a task. Jacob "served" Laban for years, working hard for him according to Genesis 31:6. It is the action of a worker, a servant, who gives their effort to a master.
2. It also designates the state of one who is politically subject, held in servitude by a power: the peoples "subject" to a king or conqueror. In Genesis 14:4, the kings had been "subjected" to Kedorlaomer; in Jeremiah 27:7, the nations will be "subjected" to the king of Babylon. It is a relationship of domination and dependence.
3. Applied to God, the word takes on a religious meaning: to "serve" God is to honor Him, to obey Him, to render worship to Him. Samuel calls Israel to "serve" the Lord alone (1 Samuel 7:3), with all their heart and trust.
4. The word can also express constraint: to be "enslaved" to someone is to be forced into it, reduced to slavery. The Israelites endured this servitude in Egypt, compelled to forced labor (Exodus 1:13-14).
H5647G.origine: The root עָבַד (a.vad) likely comes from an image of work and submission related to labor. It appears in three main forms: the simple form indicates the action itself (to work, to serve), the passive form describes what is worked or the servitude endured, the intensive form expresses constraint or oppression. The word is very ancient in the Hebrew language, and related forms are found in other Semitic languages, always with the idea of work, service, or servitude.
H5647G.emploi: The verb "serve" is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (88 occurrences). It appears mainly in Genesis, Exodus, and the prophets, particularly Jeremiah, who extensively addresses the servitude of nations. In human context, it describes the service of labor (Jacob with Laban), political subjugation (the kings under Kedorlaomer, the nations under Babylon), or forced servitude (slavery in Egypt). In a religious context, applied to God, it expresses the allegiance and worship of Israel towards the Lord. The Levites also "serve" God through the worship of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:24). The meaning varies according to context: serving a master through work, being a subject of a king, honoring God through obedience, or enduring forced servitude. This richness of meaning reflects the central place of work and obedience in the life of Israel.
H5647G.portee: This word speaks to the believer of two fundamental relationships: that of honest work and submission to the authority entrusted to them, and that, much deeper, of service to God. Serving the Lord is not a heavy burden, but an allegiance of love — Samuel calls to serve Him "with all your heart." For the disciple of Christ, it is an invitation to examine whom they truly serve: an earthly master? God alone? This word teaches that true freedom lies in voluntary service to the Lord, not in carnal independence.

sens: Work for someone else, execute their orders
Render worship to a deity or god
Fulfill a function, an office, particularly in the service of the tabernacle or the temple
Be subject to an authority, as a subject or slave
H5647H.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of work: accomplishing a task for a master or employer. It is the concrete labor of the servant or subject who fulfills a function assigned to them (Numbers 4:30: the Levites who "perform some function in the tent of meeting").

2. The word also designates worship or reverence rendered to a god—either the true God or idols. It is a religious service, a submission of the heart and body to a deity. Deuteronomy 12:30 illustrates this meaning when it speaks of how the nations "served" their gods: it is an act of worship and veneration.

3. In the context of the tabernacle and the temple, "serve" takes on a very specific shade: it is to perform the ritual service, the functions proper to the priests and Levites. The Levites are "servants" of the Lord in the sense that they exercise a sacred ministry before the ark and the altar.

4. The word can also mean to be subjected to someone, to live under their authority: this is the condition of the subject or slave towards their master or king (2 Kings 10:19 speaks of the "servants" of Baal, those who are attached to him).
H5647H.origine: The Hebrew root עָבַד (avad) literally means "to work, to labor." It is very ancient and common to Semitic languages. The agent noun "עֶבֶד" (eved) derives its meaning of "servant" or "slave" from it. The initial image is that of bent labor in the fields or in the house of a master. The word naturally expands from material work to the service of a person or a deity: to serve someone is primarily to do their work, then to obey, and finally to worship them.
H5647H.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (142 occurrences), particularly in the Pentateuch and the historical books. It appears mainly in two contexts: first, slavery and servitude in Egypt (Exodus 3:12, 4:23, etc., where Pharaoh refuses to let Israel go to "serve" God); secondly, the central question of worship and obedience to God or idols (Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges). The phrase "serve God" becomes the key expression of commitment to the Lord. Joshua 24:19 shows the tension: "You will not be able to serve the Lord, for He is a holy God." The meaning of cultic service to idols (Deuteronomy 12:30) constantly poses the choice between serving the true God or false gods. In the passages of the Pentateuch, service in the tabernacle is also a strong meaning (Numbers 3:7, 4:30, etc.).
H5647H.portee: Understanding this word opens the reader's eyes to a fundamental biblical reality: the life of the believer is a service. Serving God is not a burdensome obligation, but a response of love and obedience to the One who has set us free. Conversely, the text shows that serving idols or the powers of evil is a real and destructive slavery. This word calls us to discern where our loyalty and work lie: whom do we truly serve?

sens: Do physical work, particularly cultivate the land or engage in a trade
Work for someone else, serve them through one's labor
Perform a religious service, especially to God or in the temple
Be subject or submissive to an authority
Be worked, shaped (for the land or an object)
H5647I.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of concrete manual work: cultivating a field, plowing the land, practicing a trade. Adam is placed in the Garden of Eden to "cultivate" the soil (Genesis 2:5), and Cain is a farmer who "cultivates" the ground (Genesis 4:12). It is the image of regular physical effort that produces something.

2. The word expands to working in the service of another person: one "works" for someone by obeying them and carrying out their orders. Ziba agrees to "cultivate" the lands on behalf of his master's son (2 Samuel 9:10), which means he commits to serving this man through his labor.

3. In a religious context, "serving" God or performing a service in the temple (Levitical service) carries this same verb: it is to "work" for God, offering Him one's obedience and devotion as one would to a master.

4. The verb also expresses subjection: being subject to a king or power means being compelled to "work" for them, to be submissive and to carry out their orders (political or military sense).

5. Applied to the land, fields, or objects, "work" means to cultivate, transform, or shape them; it is the land that one "works" to make productive.
H5647I.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes effort, labor, and the action of serving. The word family includes several derivatives: "avad" produces nouns like "avodah" (work, service, worship), widely used in the Old Testament. The basic image is that of physical work that enslaves or engages: one "works" because they are obligated or because they devote themselves to someone. It is a very concrete word, rooted in the daily experience of the farmer and the servant.
H5647I.emploi: This verb is among the most frequent in the Old Testament, with about 30 major uses. It appears mainly in the accounts of origins (Genesis 2-4), where it describes the work of the soil entrusted to man, and then his painful labor after sin. The law (Deuteronomy, Exodus) uses it for daily work and Sabbath rest. The prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) take it up to describe the work of the farmer, but also to speak of the service rendered to God or the servitude imposed by a conqueror. In Proverbs, the regular work of the land is valued as a source of well-being. The word changes nuance according to the context: it is ordinary work for the farmer, service for one who obeys a master, subjection for the conquered people, and sacred worship for one who serves God.
H5647I.portee: This word brings the reader back to a fundamental biblical reality: work is not a curse in itself, but a vocation inscribed in creation—Adam must cultivate the garden even before sin. After the fall, work becomes "by the sweat of your brow," more difficult but still bearing dignity. For the Christian, this verb reminds us that serving God is also a "work," a daily offering of obedience, not just a religious feeling. It gives meaning to our ordinary labors: whether agricultural, professional, or spiritual, they are a form of service to God and to others.

sens: To load with a burden, to trouble someone with excessive work or a heavy load
To fatigue, exhaust through repeated demands
To afflict morally, to cause pain
H5647J.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to load someone with hard work or an obligation that weighs heavily. God says to Israel: "I have not burdened you with offerings" (Isaiah 43:23), which means He did not demand sacrifices beyond their strength. The word evokes the idea of overloading, placing too heavy a burden on one's shoulders.
2. From this comes the meaning of tiring, exhausting through repeated or excessive demands. This is what emerges from Isaiah 43:24: "You have troubled me with your sins, you have wearied me with your iniquities." The sins of Israel continually grieve God, like exhausting work that cannot be set down.
H5647J.origine: This Hebrew verb originally denotes imposed labor, hard work. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of servitude and obligation. In Hebrew, the same word can mean "to serve," "to work," and "to be tormented," as all these meanings revolve around imposed effort and the resulting fatigue. This is why the word applies to both work and torment: in both cases, one endures a burden.
H5647J.emploi: The verb עָבַד appears twice in Isaiah 43:23-24, in a context of God's reproach to Israel. In these verses, God asserts that He has not behaved like a tyrannical master, but rather, it is Israel who has troubled Him with their sins. The usage here is less about work or service than about moral fatigue, the torment caused by a burden that is difficult to bear. The biblical context of this chapter in Isaiah (redemption and forgiveness) sheds light on how God reproaches His people for placing the burden of unfaithfulness upon Him.
H5647J.portee: These verses reveal a profound truth: our sins affect God Himself. To say that Israel has "troubled" God means that our unfaithfulness grieves the heart of God and constitutes a burden for Him. It is a call to understand that sin is not merely an impersonal transgression, but a reality that hurts the One who loves us. This perspective invites the reader to take seriously the moral gravity of their actions and the weight they exert on the relationship with God.

sens: To create, to make, to produce something
To accomplish, to execute an action, an order
To undergo an action, to be made or transformed into something
To break apart, to destroy, to reduce to pieces
H5648.detail:
1. To create or make: the basic meaning, that of producing something, bringing it into existence. This is the work of the creator who shapes his creation. This meaning appears in administrative contexts: "Let everything that is ordered by the God of heaven be done punctually for the house of the God of heaven" (Ezra 7:23), where "to do" means to realize, to implement.
2. To accomplish, to execute: to carry out an action, a task, an order. When King Darius commands the local authorities what "they are to do regarding these elders of the Jews for the construction of this house of God" (Ezra 6:8), it is about accomplishing a specific mission. This meaning includes the idea of completing, following instructions.
3. To be made, to be realized: the passive form of the verb, when the action is accomplished upon someone or something. "The elders... complied punctually" (Ezra 6:13) shows the idea that the order is executed, realized in fact.
4. To be broken apart, to be crushed: a particular and violent meaning of the verb in Aramaic, which means to completely destroy, to reduce to pieces. "You will be broken apart, and your houses will be reduced to a heap of rubbish" (Daniel 2:5 and 3:29): this is total destruction, annihilation.
H5648.origine: The Aramaic verb עֲבַד (avad) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew verb עָשָׂה (asah), "to do." It expresses the action of creating, making, producing. In Aramaic, as in Hebrew, this very common verb is at the heart of expressing all activity: creating an object, accomplishing a task, executing a judgment. The root evokes the idea of shaping, transforming a material or a situation.
H5648.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 25 times in the Aramaic biblical texts, notably in the books of Ezra and Daniel. In Ezra, it mainly denotes the execution of royal decrees: "to do" research, "to do" constructions, "to do" according to an order. In Daniel, the meaning extends: to create a golden statue (Daniel 3:1), to accomplish an action in a dream (Daniel 4:2), to undergo an action ("to be done in pieces"). The verb can be conjugated in the passive or reflexive voice to express that something happens, is executed, or occurs to someone. Its usage thus covers the entire field of doing: creating, building, accomplishing, executing, transforming, annihilating.
H5648.portee: This verb reminds us that God orders and that His will is executed: "Let everything that is ordered by the God of heaven be done punctually" (Ezra 7:23). It invites the reader to discern how intentions become concrete acts, and how even earthly powers must conform to divine decrees. For the believer, it is a word of hope: what is ordered by God will surely be accomplished.

sens: A person in the service of a king or a master, in a relationship of dependence
One who obeys orders and carries out the work entrusted to them
A person who voluntarily places themselves under the authority of another, out of respect or fear of God
H5649.detail: 1. The servant is someone who depends on a master or a king and accepts this position. It is a well-established social status: the servants of Artaxerxes present themselves this way, acknowledging his authority (Ezra 4:11). 2. The servant executes the orders given to them and works for their master. The Chaldeans ask Nebuchadnezzar to explain his dream to them, as they are there to serve him and explain what he entrusts to them (Daniel 2:4 and 2:7). 3. The word can also refer to one who voluntarily places their trust and obedience in God. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are presented as "servants of the Most High God" (Daniel 3:26) — not enslaved, but committed to serving Him rather than bowing to idols, which shows a free and conscious obedience (Daniel 3:28).
H5649.origine: This Aramaic word עֲבַד comes from the same root as the Hebrew עֶבֶד ("servant," number H5650 in the Hebrew lexicon), but in the Aramaic form. The root evokes the idea of working or serving. In Aramaic and Hebrew, this word designates one who depends on another and works under their authority, whether for a king, a human master, or for God.
H5649.emploi: This Aramaic word appears 7 times in the Bible, exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel — the portions of the Old Testament written in Aramaic. It appears in official and political contexts: the authors of letters present themselves as "servants" of the king (Ezra 4:11, 5:11), or the Chaldeans place themselves as servants of King Nebuchadnezzar to assist him (Daniel 2:4, 2:7). But the meaning enriches in the religious context: the three young Hebrews are called "servants of the Most High God" (Daniel 3:26, 3:28), which reveals that obedience to God takes precedence over obedience to earthly powers, even royal ones. The word thus expresses both a relationship of practical dependence and a spiritual dimension of commitment to divine will.
H5649.portee: This word reminds us that every person occupies a place of dependence, either towards human authorities or towards God. For the believer, it shows that serving God is not a humiliating servitude, but a position of honor and protection — as God preserved His "servants" in the furnace. It is a call to recognize our dependence on God and the pride there is in placing our trust in Him rather than bowing to false gods or the powers of the world.

sens: A person who is enslaved, belonging to a master and must obey him
Subject of a king, a people placed under his authority
One who voluntarily places himself at the service of someone, in an attitude of respect or submission
Worshiper, one who renders worship to God
Prophet or minister chosen by God to fulfill His will
Polite formula by which one humbly addresses someone
H5650.detail:
1. A servant is primarily someone who belongs to a master and must work for him, as Canaan is cursed to become "the slave of slaves" to his brothers (Genesis 9:25) — this is a condition of total dependence. This can be a slave in the strict sense of the term, or a worker temporarily hired, like one who agrees to sell himself to pay off a debt (Leviticus 25:39).
2. Next, the servant refers to the subjects of a king: Joab asks the king why he would cause "all the servants of his lord" to sin, meaning the people placed under his authority (1 Chronicles 21:3).
3. The term also applies to one who voluntarily places himself under the authority of another, out of respect or devotion — it is almost a polite formula among the patriarchs who say "your servant" to refer to themselves when addressing someone greater.
4. In a spiritual sense, a servant of God is one who worships Him and obeys Him with all his heart — David prays to God to remember the word he gave to "your servant David" (1 Kings 8:26), acknowledging his dependence on God.
5. Finally, some servants are chosen by God for special missions — prophets, Levites — who bear the honorable title of "servant of the Lord."
6. Among equals, it is a modest formula: "your servant" can simply mean "me" when one speaks humbly of oneself.
H5650.origine: The Hebrew word עֶבֶד comes from a root meaning "to work" or "to serve." It is a fundamental word in the Bible, expressing the idea of dependence and subjugation, but also of voluntary devotion. The same root produces other words related to work and service. In the Greek Old Testament, this Hebrew word is regularly translated by the Greek word doulos (slave) or diakonos (servant), showing that the concept transfers from one language to another without losing its richness.
H5650.emploi: The word appears more than 700 times in the Old Testament, making it a key word. It is found everywhere: among the patriarchs who respectfully speak of themselves (Genesis 32:4-5), in laws regarding temporary service (Leviticus 25:39), in the history of kings and their officials, and especially in the Psalms and the Prophets where the servant of God becomes a title of glory. The meaning varies: initially very concrete (a servant who belongs to a master), it gradually becomes more theological and honorable. Even a king can refer to himself as a servant of the Lord to express his obedience to God. This shift shows that in the Bible, serving God is not a humiliation, but the highest honor.
H5650.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on what it means to be in the service of God. It is not a shameful slavery, but a calling of devotion and obedience. Jesus Himself will present Himself as the servant par excellence, the one who humbles Himself to serve and save. Understanding this word helps to grasp the hidden nobility of serving God and others in faith.

sens: Father of Gaal, a man who rebelled against Abimelech during the time of the Judges
H5651G.detail: Ebed is a man mentioned only as the father of Gaal in the account from the book of Judges. His son Gaal appears in Shechem during the time of the Judges, leading a revolt against Abimelech who had proclaimed himself king. Although Ebed himself does not appear directly in the action, his name is repeated each time his son Gaal is mentioned ("Gaal, son of Ebed"), linking the rebel to his family and emphasizing the heritage of the lineage. The text presents him solely through this genealogical link.
H5651G.origine: The name Ebed means "servant" in Hebrew, derived from the Hebrew root עבד (avad) which means "to serve" or "to be a servant." This word is very common in the Old Testament to designate a servant, a slave, or someone who serves. The irony of the name "servant" given to the father of a rebel who refuses to serve Abimelech enriches the narrative of Judges 9.
H5651G.emploi: Ebed appears only five times in the Bible, all in the book of Judges chapter 9, where he is systematically presented as the father of Gaal (Judges 9:26, 9:28, 9:30, 9:31, 9:35). These mentions focus around the conflict that Gaal provokes in Shechem against Abimelech. Ebed himself does not speak or act in the text; he is simply mentioned to identify the family origin of his rebellious son.

sens: Man from the family of Adin who returned from exile with Ezra
H5651H.detail: Ebed is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile at the time of Ezra. He is presented as the son of Jonathan and belongs to the family of Adin. He returns from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra and leads fifty men from his family (Ezra 8:6).
H5651H.origine: The name Ebed comes from Hebrew and means "servant" or "slave." It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several men. The name recalls the fundamental identity of the people of Israel: to serve God and be His servant.
H5651H.emploi: Ebed appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:6. He is one of the family leaders whose name Ezra lists during the organization of the return from exile to Jerusalem. His appearance in this official list shows that he held a respectable place among the returned exiles, significant enough to lead a group of fifty men.

sens: Productive activity, sustained effort to accomplish a task
Work produced by effort, a concrete result
In a figurative sense: an enterprise, project, or ongoing affair
H5652.detail:
1. Work primarily refers to the activity itself, the effort one expends to accomplish something. It is the daily labor, whether manual or intellectual. In Ecclesiastes 9:1, the preacher speaks of his "works" of investigation and examination: he has applied his heart to understand what happens under the sun, and this sustained effort is his work.
2. The word can also refer to the work resulting from effort, what has been produced or completed. It is the tangible fruit of effort.
3. More broadly, it is used for an enterprise or a matter, something that has been put in motion and is being pursued.
H5652.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of shaping, creating, or producing through effort. It is very ancient and very common in the Bible. It appears in various forms in Hebrew: עָבַד (the verb "to work") and other derivatives sharing the same root. In the Greek Old Testament, it is often translated by Greek words also denoting work or activity.
H5652.emploi: This word appears once in our texts, in Ecclesiastes 9:1, where the preacher speaks of his works of investigation and reflection. It is in a context of wisdom: he has devoted all his efforts to examining and understanding the human condition and the role of wisdom and justice in the world. His "works" — his efforts of reflection — are in the hand of God: it is He who has set them in motion, who directs them, and who disposes of them. This passage emphasizes that all labor, even intellectual and spiritual, ultimately falls under God's authority.
H5652.portee: This word reminds the reader that work is not a vain or meaningless burden: it is part of God's design. Even when one struggles to understand the order of the world or to accomplish their task, the believer can trust in God who holds the labor in His hand. This encourages a perspective of trust instead of discouragement: our work matters because God has mastery over it.

sens: father of Adoniram, officer of King Solomon
H5653G.detail: Abda is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of King Solomon. He is the father of Adoniram, who held an important position at the royal court: he was in charge of the kingdom's taxes (1 Kings 4:6). His name means "servant of Jehovah" in Hebrew, but the Bible tells us nothing else about his life or personal role.
H5653G.origine: The name Abda is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ab" meaning "servant" or "slave," and "da" formed from "Jah" (the divine name). Thus, his name expresses a relationship of dependence on God — the idea of being in service to Jehovah. One of his descendants, the Levite Obadiah, bears a very similar name, also related to this same concept of divine service.
H5653G.emploi: Abda appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Kings 4:6. He is simply identified as the father of Adoniram, who was a respected officer during Solomon's reign, responsible for collecting taxes from the people. This unique mention firmly places him in the time of the united monarchy, before the division of the kingdom into two after Solomon's death.

sens: Levite of the time of the return from exile
son of Shammua and grandson of Galal
temple musician in charge of leading praise
H5653H.detail: Abda is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to the service of the temple. He lived at the time of the return from exile, after the Israelites were able to return from Babylon. His name means "servant of Jehovah," which reflects his sacred vocation. In Nehemiah 11:17, he is presented as the son of Shammua, himself the son of Galal, and as a chief responsible for leading the praise in prayer — that is, directing the singing and music during temple services.
H5653H.origine: The name Abda comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to serve" or "to be a servant." It is formed from "Abd" (servant) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah), hence the complete meaning: "servant of Jehovah." This same Abda is also called Obadiah (עֹבַדְיָהוּ) elsewhere in Scripture, Obadiah being the full form of the same name — "Obadiah" literally means "servant of Jehovah." Names composed with this root were common among the Levites and temple servants.
H5653H.emploi: Abda appears only once in the canonical Bible, in Nehemiah 11:17. He is mentioned in the list of Levites who returned to Jerusalem after the exile, among those who had received important roles in the restoration of temple worship. His role as chief responsible for leading the praise in prayer shows that he was a recognized musician and leader, responsible for directing liturgical songs. The presence of his name in this genealogical list underscores the importance of the role of musician Levites in the reorganization of the temple after the return from captivity.
H5653H.portee: The name Abda reminds us that serving God in praise and sacred music was an honorable and often hereditary function (his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather descended from Levite leaders). For the believer, this example shows that the organized praise of the temple was entrusted to men of faith, whose genealogy attested to the continuity of divine service even after the trial of exile.

sens: Levite who welcomed the Ark of the Lord at Gath
Gatekeeper and musician of the temple under the reign of David
H5654.detail:
1. Obed-Edon is first known as the Gittite (man from Gath) who received the Ark of God into his home when David did not dare to bring it into Jerusalem after the death of Uzzah. The ark remained in his house for three months, and during that time the Lord blessed Obed-Edon and all that belonged to him (2 Samuel 6:10-12 and 1 Chronicles 13:14).
2. He later became a Levite from the family of Jeduthun, a musician and gatekeeper of the temple. He played the harp during ceremonies and kept the doors of the house of God with his many sons and brothers (1 Chronicles 15:21; 16:38).
H5654.origine: His name means "servant of Edom." He belonged to the tribe of Levi, the priestly tribe of Israel, and was the son of Jeduthun, one of the masters of music in the temple. Despite his nickname of Gittite (from Gath), he was a Levite and held important religious functions in the temple worship.
H5654.emploi: Obed-Edon appears fifteen times in Scripture, primarily in 2 Samuel 6 and 1 Chronicles 13-26. He is first mentioned as the one with whom the Ark of God rests (2 Samuel 6:10), before it is transported to Jerusalem by David. He is then presented as a musician and gatekeeper of the temple, responsible for leading the singing with harps and guarding the doors of the house of God (1 Chronicles 15:21; 16:38). He had eight sons who also held important positions in the service of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:4-8). His story shows how a responsibility towards divine worship brings the blessing of the Lord.
H5654.portee: The story of Obed-Edon teaches that serving God, even in seemingly modest tasks, attracts divine blessing. The respect due to the Ark of the Covenant — the presence of God — is manifested by the prosperity that descends upon his house. His example invites the reader to seek God's honor rather than their own glory, and to faithfully exercise the spiritual responsibilities that God entrusts.

sens: father of the character Shelemiah mentioned during the time of the prophet Jeremiah
H5655.detail: Abdeel is a man of whom we know only one fact: he is the father of Shelemiah. This Shelemiah appears in the story of the scroll of Jeremiah, when King Jehoiakim orders several officials, including the son of Abdeel, to capture the prophet Jeremiah and his secretary Baruch (Jeremiah 36:26). Although his son received an order from the king, the Lord protected the prophet and his secretary from these men.
H5655.origine: The name Abdeel means "servant of God" in Hebrew: it combines two roots, one meaning "servant" and the other "God." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the piety of the one who bore it by placing him under divine authority.
H5655.emploi: Abdeel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 36:26. He appears as the father of Shelemiah, one of the three officials whom King Jehoiakim sent to arrest Jeremiah after hearing the scroll containing the prophet's words read. His name is known to us only through this familial link, in a context where royalty opposed the divine message.

sens: work, labor that must be accomplished
servitude, subjection to foreign domination
work assigned to a charge or function
service rendered to God through prayer and worship
H5656G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the work, the task that one executes. Jacob asks Laban: "Complete the week with this one, and we will also give you the other for the service you will perform for me for another seven years" (Genesis 29:27). It is simply the agreed labor.

2. It takes on a harsher meaning when it designates servitude, especially imposed slavery. The Israelites in Egypt "groaned under the servitude" (Exodus 2:23) — not a chosen work, but a yoke that weighs down. After the Exodus, the people ask the king: "Lighten this harsh servitude and the heavy yoke" (1 Kings 12:4).

3. In Israel, the word also describes the service of worship, the office in the temple: "all his service" (Exodus 35:21) refers to all the work and rites of the sanctuary.

4. By extension, it is the service rendered to God Himself — obedience, prayer, worship — to which the believer commits.
H5656G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root עבד (avad), which means "to work" or "to serve." It also gives rise to the word עֶבֶד (éved), "servant" or "slave." The central idea is one of subjection to a task: one works under the authority of someone else, like a servant or a captive. The image is that of imposed or consented labor.
H5656G.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the accounts of the Exodus and in texts about Egypt, the temple, and royalty. It is used for Jacob's work for Laban (Genesis), the servitude in Egypt (Exodus), the service of the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Chronicles), and the corvée work of kings (Kings, Chronicles). Isaiah uses it to announce deliverance: "The LORD will give him rest, away from servitude" (14:3). The word shifts from the concrete (work done) to the figurative (yoke endured or service offered).
H5656G.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that servitude is a reality of the world — sometimes unjust, always demanding — but also that true service, the one offered to God, is liberating. It awakens compassion for those who suffer and a consciousness that our service to God is not a burden, but a response of love to the freedom He gives.

sens: Work or task performed for someone
Charge or function assigned to a person in a community
Religious service, work done at the tabernacle or temple to honor God
Work of a captive or enslaved person, often painful and obligatory
H5656H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the work or concrete task that one performs: it is the action of serving, the labor accomplished. In Exodus 27:19, all the utensils intended for the "service" of the tabernacle are objects that serve to carry out the ritual tasks.
2. It is also a specific charge or function entrusted to someone: in Numbers 4:23, those "fit to perform some function in the tent of meeting" are counted, meaning the Levites capable of certain specific tasks of worship.
3. The word particularly applies to religious service at the tabernacle and then at the temple: in Numbers 18:6, the Levites are "given as a gift to perform the service of the tent of meeting," this special work that honors God and maintains communion with Him.
4. It can also evoke the work of a captive or slave, the imposed and obligatory labor; the Exodus itself speaks of the "service" in Egypt. It is constrained work, without freedom.
H5656H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to work" or "to serve." It is related to the idea of rendering a service, of employing oneself for someone else. In ancient Greek, this word is generally translated as "diakonia" or "leitourgia" (liturgy), which also evoke service, particularly the religious service rendered to the gods or to the community.
H5656H.emploi: The word appears 73 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the history of the temple (Chronicles). It primarily designates the material work of the Levites at the tabernacle: transporting, setting up, and maintaining the tent and its objects (Numbers 3-4), purifying the holy things (1 Chronicles 23:28), performing the daily sacrifices (2 Chronicles 8:14). It also applies to the services of worship and sacred music (1 Chronicles 6:32, 25:1). Sometimes it evokes the imposed work of captives or corvée laborers (Numbers 16:9). The meaning nuances: from manual and organized work (Numbers 7:5) to liturgical and spiritual service (Numbers 18:6-7), passing through the charge and responsibility entrusted to each according to their place.
H5656H.portee: This word reminds the believer that the service of God is not a secondary activity, but a serious, organized, and sacred work. It shows that everyone has their part in community and cultic service: a function, a role, a responsibility before God. It is also an invitation to see daily work not as a curse, but as a possible form of service towards God and others.

sens: Physical effort required of someone to accomplish a task
Imposed labor of authority, particularly that of a slave or captive
Task, work to be executed, with emphasis on its result
Work prohibited during holy days, contrast between ordinary work and sacred rest
Service rendered to God in worship or obedience
H5656I.detail:
1. Work designates the physical effort and activity necessary to create something or accomplish a task. In Exodus 1:14, the Egyptians impose "hard work in clay and bricks" on the Hebrews: it is the concrete labor of the construction site.
2. This word particularly evokes imposed work, that which the slave or captive endures without freedom. When Pharaoh demands increased "work" from the Hebrews (Exodus 5:9), it is a brutal burden imposed against their will.
3. Work can also designate the finished product, the result of the effort: in Exodus 36:1 and 39:32, it is "all the work" of the tabernacle that the artisans have accomplished.
4. In the religious calendar (Leviticus 23:21, Numbers 28:18), "servile work" is that which is prohibited on holy days: it is ordinary, earthly work, contrasting with rest and worship.
5. Service to God shares the same root: accomplishing the work of worship, obeying what is commanded.
H5656I.origine: The Hebrew word עֲבֹדָה comes from the root עָבַד (to serve, to be a servant). This root evokes the fundamental idea of being at the service of someone, of doing what one is asked. Work is thus, for the one who endures it, a form of servitude: one "works for" someone else. The same family includes עֶבֶד (slave, servant) and עַבְדוּת (servitude). In Greek, this word is often translated as douleía (servitude) or érgon (work).
H5656I.emploi: This word appears about 30 times in the Bible, concentrated mainly in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, where it describes either the work imposed on the Hebrews in Egypt (Exodus 1:14, 5:9), or the construction work of the tabernacle (Exodus 35:24, 36:1, 39:32), or the prohibition of work on holy days (Leviticus 23:21, Numbers 28:18, 29:35). It is also found in Psalm 104:14 to designate the needs that grass provides, and in the prophets (Isaiah 28:21, Ezekiel 29:18) to speak of human labor in general. The word thus shifts from servile and oppressive work to constructive work and the rest one takes from it.
H5656I.portee: Meditating on this word invites the believer to see work not as a mere chore, but as a reality that God frames through rest and worship. The holy days remind us that not all work exhausts life: there is a time for rest and for serving God. And for those who suffer under an unjust yoke, the word work in Exodus speaks of liberation and restored dignity.

sens: Quantity of servants or slaves in the service of a household
Large number of personnel under submission
Multitude of people attached to a master
H5657.detail: 1. The word literally designates a troop or a staff of servants — people employed in the service of a household. In Genesis 26:14, Isaac possessed "a large number of servants," which testified to his wealth and power: the more servants one had, the more powerful and honored one was. 2. The term evokes the idea of a mass of personnel, a crowd of slaves or attendants.
