Job, in the account of his prosperity, is described as having "a very large number of servants" (Job 1:3), placing him among the greatest men of the East. 3. By extension, the word emphasizes the multitude and numerical importance: it is less about who they are than their massive quantity, a symbol of dominance and resources.
H5657.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to work" or "to serve." It has also given rise to the word "avodah" (service, work). The initial image is one of labor and subjugation: it moves from the work itself to the multitude of those who work for you. It is a concrete word that enumerates measurable material wealth — not abstract.
H5657.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to enumerate the extraordinary wealth of a wise and blessed man of God. In Genesis 26:14, Isaac is envied by the Philistines precisely because of his many servants — a sign of his prosperity. In Job 1:3, the same trait is used to portray Job before his trial, showing that he was "the most distinguished of all the sons of the East." In both cases, the possession of many servants is an indicator of divine blessing and eminent social status.
H5657.portee: For the biblical reader, these verses remind us that wealth in the Old Testament is not measured solely in gold or land, but also in human resources — in the ability to command and support a household. It is a sign of God's blessing and the wisdom that accompanies one who prospers according to His will. It also shows that prosperity is not just personal, but affects an entire network of servants who depend on the master.

sens: City of the tribe of Asher assigned to the Gershonite Levites
H5658G.detail: Abdon is a city located in the tribe of Asher, in the promised land. It was assigned to the Levites of the family of Gershon, who descended from Levi and had religious and priestly functions. Its name means "servile" or "servitude," perhaps evoking religious service. The city is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in relation to this territorial assignment to the Levites (Joshua 21:30 and 1 Chronicles 6:74), which shows its importance as a Levitical center. It was located about 16 kilometers north of Acco, in the northern part of the Israelite territory.
H5658G.origine: The name Abdon comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to serve" or "to be servile," from which the idea of servitude or service derives. This name is well-suited for a city assigned to the Levites, who were the servants of the temple and divine worship. The city also bears the alternative name Ebron.
H5658G.emploi: Abdon appears only twice in the Bible, both times in administrative lists of Levitical cities. In Joshua 21:30, it is listed among the cities assigned to the sons of Gershon, Levites of the tribe of Asher. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 6:74 repeats the same list. These two occurrences show that Abdon was a refuge city and Levitical residence, where Levites carried out their religious functions while living among the people of Israel.

sens: Judge of Israel during the time of the Judges
Son of Hillel of Pirathon
H5658H.detail:
1. Abdon is a judge of Israel who governed the people during the period of the Judges, before the monarchy. He succeeded Jephthah and judged the people before Samuel established the monarchy in Israel (Judges 12:13-15).

2. He is specifically identified as the son of Hillel and from Pirathon, a city in the region of Ephraim. It is in Pirathon that he is buried after his death, on the hill of the Amalekites (Judges 12:15).
H5658H.origine: The name Abdon means "servile" or "servitude" in Hebrew, derived from a root that evokes the idea of serving. In the Old Testament, this name carries the image of a man called to serve God and His people, which corresponds to his role as a judge.
H5658H.emploi: Abdon is mentioned twice in the Holy Scriptures, only in the book of Judges. He is presented as one of the twelve great judges who led Israel after the conquest of Canaan and before the establishment of the royal monarchy. The only details we have about him concern his genealogy (son of Hillel) and his place of origin (Pirathon in Ephraim). His ministry as a judge, like that of his predecessors, was to exercise judicial and military authority to lead and defend the people of Israel.
H5658H.portee: Abdon represents the faithfulness of a generation of leaders who served God and His people during a crucial period in Israel's history. His name, meaning "servitude," invites the reader to reflect on what it truly means to serve — not as a slave submitted by force, but as a humble leader putting the good of the people before his personal interests. His life reminds us that serving God involves dedication to those we are to lead.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
H5658I.detail: 1. Abdon is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 8:23, as the son of Shashak and brother of several other Benjamites including Ishpan, Eber, and Eliel. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, when the kingdom of Israel was split between the North and the South.
H5658I.origine: The name Abdon comes from Hebrew and means "servile" or "one who serves." It is formed from a root that evokes the idea of servitude and obedience. It is a name that recalls the relationship of service, characteristic of Hebrew names from this period.
H5658I.emploi: Abdon is cited only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:23, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. This passage enumerates the sons and descendants of Shashak, a head of the Benjamite family. Abdon appears there simply as a name among others, with no action or particular event reported about him. His mention in these genealogical lists shows the importance that the Bible attaches to the continuity of family lines, even for minor characters.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
Judge of Israel during the time of the judges
H5658J.detail:
1. Abdon is primarily a man of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogies of the people of Israel. He appears as the son of Abiel and Maacah, brother to a large family including Kis, Ner, Zur, Baal, Nadab, and others. His names are listed in 1 Chronicles 8 and 9, documents that record the ancestors of the families of Israel during the time of the united monarchy under David and Solomon.
2. Abdon is also known as a judge of Israel during the time of the judges, the military and spiritual leaders who governed Israel before the monarchy. Although few details are given about his ministry, he represents one of those figures who guided the people according to the order established by God.
H5658J.origine: The name Abdon means "servile" or "one who serves." It derives from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of service or servitude. This name reflects an important theological reality: the one who bears this name is devoted to service, reminding us that in the tradition of Israel, true honor lies in serving God and the people.
H5658J.emploi: Abdon appears in two main references in 1 Chronicles, where his name is included in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as the firstborn son of someone (in 1 Chronicles 8:30 and 9:36), integrated into the lists of descent that establish the genealogies of the people in view of the return from exile. These two verses seem to document the same genealogy. Beyond these genealogical mentions, Abdon is also designated as a judge of Israel during the period of the judges, although the details of his activity are not reported in the preserved biblical text. He embodies one of those figures from Israel's past who led the people according to divine will.
H5658J.portee: Abdon reminds us that the history of Israel is composed of many figures whose names alone have reached us, but whose faithfulness to God marked their generation. His name, meaning "servile," invites the reader to meditate on true service: the one who recognizes their place before God is free to serve effectively. For the Christian, this ancient figure illustrates how God has always raised faithful leaders to guide His people according to His will.

sens: An officer of King Josiah of Judah
A judge of Israel during the time of the judges
A Benjamite of the tribe of Benjamin
A Gibeonite from the family of Gideon
A city in the tribe of Asher
H5658K.detail:
1. Abdon is a royal officer who served King Josiah around 620 B.C. He was the son of Micah and was ordered by the king to investigate the Book of the Law discovered in the Temple (2 Chronicles 34:20); he was a trusted man of the king.
2. Abdon was also one of the judges of Israel at a time when the people did not yet have a king, probably before the unified monarchy.
3. A Benjamite named Abdon was the son of Shashak and belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.
4. A Gibeonite of the same name was the son of Jehiel and the grandson of Gideon, the famous warrior who delivered Israel from the Midianites.
5. Abdon also refers to a city in the tribe of Asher, located in northern Israel, about 16 kilometers north of Acre, and it was assigned to the Levites descended from Gershon.
H5658K.origine: The name Abdon means "servile" or "servant," derived from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of servitude. It is a name that reflects the humility or status of the one who bears it. The same name has been used for several important figures in the history of Israel, indicating that it was a common and respected name.
H5658K.emploi: In the Old Testament, the name Abdon refers to several important people and a place at different times in Israel's history. The most notable usage is that of Abdon, officer of King Josiah, mentioned in 2 Chronicles 34:20, where he receives a mission from the king to consult the prophetess Huldah about the discovered Book of the Law. Abdon was also a judge of Israel, placing him among the leaders of the people before the establishment of the monarchy. The multiplicity of characters bearing this name shows that it was a respected designation in several tribes and at different periods.
H5658K.portee: This name reminds us that God has used faithful servants, even modestly named, to accomplish His will in the history of Israel. The officer Abdon serving King Josiah illustrates how men can cooperate in the discovery and obedience to the Word of God.

sens: State of one who is a slave, subject to a master
Condition of servitude, lack of freedom
Oppression or domination of a people by a foreign power
H5659.detail:
1. Servitude is the state of one who belongs to a master and must obey him without freedom. It is the fate of slaves in the literal sense. The Hebrew word comes from the root "slave" and denotes this condition of total dependence.
2. More broadly, it encompasses any form of servitude or loss of freedom — being chained, dominated, deprived of autonomy. When Israel returns from exile in Babylon, although they have returned to their land, the people remain under the yoke of the kings of Persia: this is still a servitude (Ezra 9:9).
3. Historically, it refers to the oppression of a people by a foreign power: the Israelites exiled in Babylon had to live in servitude, far from their land and temple. Nehemiah 9:17 recalls how the ancestors, in the desert, wanted to return to that servitude of Egypt — a refusal of the freedom that God offered them.
H5659.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "avad" (עבד), which means "to serve" or "to be a slave." The suffix "ut" (וּת) forms an abstract noun denoting the state or condition. It is the same root that gives "eved" (עבד), the slave or servant. The word evokes complete subjugation, with no possibility of refusal.
H5659.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the post-exilic books (Ezra and Nehemiah), echoes of captivity and the reconstruction of the temple. It first describes the concrete situation of the people returned from Babylon: although spared and brought back to Jerusalem, Israel still lives under the authority of the Persian kings, which is a form of servitude (Ezra 9:8-9). The word also takes on a spiritual value: refusing God's freedom to return to a past servitude is to choose the slavery of sin and distance from God (Nehemiah 9:17). In these three usages, the term always expresses an involuntary and painful dependence.
H5659.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true freedom comes from God alone. Even when circumstances seem difficult or when we are "subjected" to human powers, we must not forget that God never abandons us to servitude and always offers a form of life and hope. It is also a warning: turning away from God to return to old spiritual servitudes — sin, idolatry, self-esteem — is to refuse the freedom He offers us.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Merari, ancestor of the singer Ethan
H5660G.detail: Abdi is a Levite from the family of Merari mentioned in the genealogical account of the temple singers. He is the father of Kish and the grandfather of Ethan, who led the singing in the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 6:44). His name means "servant of the Lord," which fits his role in divine service.
H5660G.origine: The name Abdi comes from Hebrew and literally means "servant of the Lord" ("abd" = servant, and the suffix "i" = my). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that includes a reference to God. This type of name was common in Israel to express dedication to God from birth.
H5660G.emploi: Abdi is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:44, within the genealogy of the musicians of the temple during the time of the divided monarchy. He is listed in the lineage of the Merarite Levites who were tasked with singing in the sanctuary. The text presents him as a link in an honorable genealogical chain: he is the son of Malluch and the father of Kish, whose son Ethan became a famous singer.

sens: man of the tribe of Levi, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H5660H.detail: Abdi is a Levite from the family of Merari, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the father of Kis, who is also a Levite. Both are cited during the purification of the Temple under King Hezekiah of Judah, when the Levites rose up to carry out this holy task (2 Chronicles 29:12). The name means "servant of the Lord" in Hebrew, which well characterizes the role of the Levites in the service of worship.
H5660H.origine: The name Abdi comes from Hebrew and literally means "servant of Jehovah" (the Lord). It is formed from the root "abd" (servant) and the abbreviated divine name. This name expresses the vocation of the Levites: to be in the service of God and worship in the Temple.
H5660H.emploi: Abdi appears only once in Scripture, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He is mentioned as the father of Kis in the context of the religious reform of King Hezekiah, when the Levites mobilized to cleanse and consecrate the Temple of Jerusalem again. This appearance shows the active role of the Levites from the family of Merari in the religious history of Judah.

sens: man of the tribe of Levi, from the family of Merari, living during the time of the exile and return
H5660I.detail: 1. Abdi is a Levite from the family of Merari mentioned in Ezra 10:26 as having taken a foreign wife. This is a detail from the return from exile, when the people of Judah returned from Babylon and had to separate from these marriages contracted during exile. His name means "servant of Jehovah" in Hebrew.
H5660I.origine: The name Abdi (עַבְדִּי) is composed of "eved" (servant) and the suffix "-i" (my). It is a theophoric name formed on the idea of being a servant of God, a common name in Israel among Levites who were dedicated to the service of the temple. The family of Merari was one of the three branches of the Levites responsible for transporting and maintaining the tabernacle.
H5660I.emploi: Abdi appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:26. He is presented among the sons of Elam who had married foreign women and who, at Ezra's command, had to separate from them at the time of the return from exile. This passage shows a critical moment in Israel's history, where the reconstitution of the pure religious community required this radical break. Abdi represents these ordinary Israelites affected by these decisions.

sens: man of the tribe of Gad during the time of the divided monarchy
H5661.detail: Abdiel is a man of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Guni and the father of Ahi (1 Chronicles 5:15). He lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms, under the reign of King Jotham of Judah. Abdiel and his family settled in the region of Bashan, a fertile territory east of the Jordan, which belonged to the tribe of Gad.
H5661.origine: The name Abdiel means "servant of God": "abd" means servant or slave, and "El" refers to God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in Israel to express the relationship between a person and the Lord.
H5661.emploi: Abdiel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:15, where he is cited in a genealogy of the tribe of Gad. This passage lists the ancestors and descendants of Abdiel to establish the lineages and family leaders of the territory. His only role in the biblical narrative is to situate the genealogy of his son Ahi in the history of the people of Gad.

sens: chief of the house of King Ahab, a pious man who saved prophets
the prophet author of the book of Obadiah, who prophesies against Edom
several other characters bearing this name in the history of Israel
H5662G.detail:
1. Obadiah is first known as the steward of the royal house of King Ahab of Israel. He is a man of great piety who, during the persecution led by Queen Jezebel against the prophets of the Lord, hid more than a hundred prophets in caves and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:3-4). His name appears in the account where King Ahab charges him to go throughout the land in search of water and pastures during a time of drought (1 Kings 18:5-6), and it is Obadiah who meets the prophet Elijah on the road and brings him back to the king (1 Kings 18:7).
2. Obadiah is also the name of the fourth of the twelve minor prophets, the author of a prophetic book that contains words against the kingdom of Edom. Although the personal details of this prophet are unknown, he likely lived during the time of the great prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.
3. The name Obadiah is borne by several other characters in the Old Testament: tribal leaders, Levites, descendants of David, and other figures in the history of Israel, showing that it was a common name among the faithful of Israel.
H5662G.origine: The name Obadiah comes from Hebrew and literally means "servant of Jehovah" or "servant of the Lord." It is composed of two elements: "ebed" (servant) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). This name expresses the idea of a life entirely devoted to the service of God, which perfectly corresponds to the character of the first Obadiah known in Scripture, who risked his life to protect the prophets of the Lord.
H5662G.emploi: Obadiah primarily appears in the account of 1 Kings 18, where he is presented as chief of Ahab's house and a God-fearing man. In this passage, Obadiah exercises authority within the royal palace while remaining a faithful worshiper of the Lord, showing that it is possible to serve an ungodly king while remaining pious. The name Obadiah is then borne by at least twelve other people in the Old Testament, including a famous prophet, Levites, tribal leaders, and descendants of David. This multiplicity of namesakes reflects the popularity of the name in Israelite tradition and its association with faithfulness to God.
H5662G.portee: The example of Obadiah, chief of Ahab's house, teaches that faithfulness to God can be lived even in a position of servant or subordinate to an ungodly king. His courage in hiding the prophets at the risk of his life shows that the fear of the Lord takes precedence over the fear of men. His name, which means "servant of the Lord," reminds the reader that true service consists of obeying God rather than earthly authorities that oppose His will.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
The prophet among the Twelve Minor Prophets, author of a prophecy against Edom
Chief of the palace of King Ahab of Israel, protector of the prophets pursued by Jezebel
H5662H.detail:
1. Abdias is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament. In 1 Chronicles 3:21, he appears as a descendant of Hanania, part of the lineage of David during the time of the divided monarchy.

2. The most famous Abdias is the prophet, fourth of the Twelve Minor Prophets. Although the details of his personal life are unknown, historians assume he lived during the time of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. His prophetic book contains a message of judgment against the kingdom of Edom.

3. Another notable Abdias was the chief of the palace (steward) of King Ahab of Israel. This man risked his own life to hide more than a hundred prophets of the Lord during the persecution led by Queen Jezebel.
H5662H.origine: The name Abdias means "servant of the Lord" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "ebed" (servant) and "yah" (abbreviation of the divine Name). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it, reminding that the bearer recognizes himself as a servant of the Lord. This type of name was common in Israel to express dependence on God.
H5662H.emploi: The name Abdias is borne by many different people in the Old Testament: a prophet (whose book bears the title "Abdias"), a chief of the palace of King Ahab, an officer of David, Levites, tribal leaders, and officials during the time of Nehemiah. The mention in 1 Chronicles 3:21 places him among the descendants of David. This multiplicity of bearers of the name indicates its popularity in Israel, reflecting the piety of families who gave it to their children.
H5662H.portee: The name Abdias reminds believers that bearing the name of the Lord in their lives — symbolically or literally — implies recognizing oneself as His servant. The prophet Abdias, in particular, teaches through his ministry that the Lord judges the pride of nations and that no kingdom can stand against Him. The steward Abdias of Ahab's palace shows that one can serve God with courage even in a hostile and idolatrous environment.

sens: A man from the tribe of Issachar during the time of the divided monarchy
H5662I.detail: Abdias is a man from the tribe of Issachar mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:3. He is the son of Uzzi and brother of Micael, Joel, and Ishijah. These five brothers are designated as leaders of their tribe, indicating that they held a position of responsibility and authority within the community of Israel.
H5662I.origine: The name Abdias means "servant of the Lord" in Hebrew (עֹבַדְיָ֫הוּ). It is composed of the word עֹבֵד (servant) and the divine name יָה (Yah, contracted form of the Lord). This name has been borne by several important characters in biblical history, including the fourth of the twelve minor prophets, but also by many other lesser-known men in the genealogies of Israel.
H5662I.emploi: Abdias is the name borne by at least thirteen people in the Bible. The one mentioned here in 1 Chronicles 7:3 is a leader of the tribe of Issachar, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He appears in the genealogies preserved after the exile, showing the importance that the Hebrews placed on maintaining genealogical records for each tribe. Among the other Abdias in the Bible, the most famous is the prophet whose book is among the twelve minor prophets and prophesies against Edom, and another who was chief of the house of King Ahab, saving more than a hundred prophets during the persecution of Jezebel.

sens: A man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Atzel, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H5662J.detail: Abdias is a man belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of King Saul. He is named as one of the six sons of Atzel, alongside his brothers Azrikam, Bocru, Ishmael, Sheariah, and Hanan (1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44). This name, although borne by more than thirteen different people in the Bible, here designates a simple member of the Benjaminite royal lineage, with no notable public function mentioned.
H5662J.origine: The name Abdias means "servant of God" or "servant of Jehovah" in Hebrew. It comes from the combination of two elements: "ebed" (servant) and "Yah" (abbreviation of Jehovah). This theophoric name expresses a relationship of dependence and devotion to God, a common characteristic of Hebrew names from the monarchical period.
H5662J.emploi: Abdias is a name borne by many people in the Hebrew Bible. The Abdias mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:38 and repeated in 9:44 is simply listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, as one of the sons of Atzel. This genealogical passage establishes his place in the lineage of Saul, without providing other biographical details. The same name is borne by other important characters, including the prophet Abdias (fourth of the twelve minor prophets), but these are distinct homonyms.

sens: A Levite during the Exile and Return, son of Schemaiah
H5662K.detail: Abdias is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, including a Levite mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:16 as "Abdias, son of Schemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun." He also appears in Nehemiah 12:25 among the gatekeepers who guarded the thresholds of the gates. This Levite lived at the time when the Israelites were returning from Babylonian exile and reorganizing the Temple worship. His name means "servant of Jehovah" and expresses the devotion to God expected of a man holding a position in the house of God.
H5662K.origine: The name Abdias comes from Hebrew and literally means "servant of Jehovah" ("abd" = servant, "Jah" = God). It is a theophoric name, composed of the divine name, common among Levites and men of faith in the Old Testament. The Levite Abdias mentioned here bears this name which expresses his consecration to the service of the Lord.
H5662K.emploi: Abdias is a name borne by at least thirteen distinct individuals in the Old Testament. This one appears in two contexts: first in 1 Chronicles 9:16 as part of the genealogy of the Levites who returned to Jerusalem after the exile, and then in Nehemiah 12:25 among the gatekeepers of the Temple during the time of Nehemiah. Both references show that he was a man holding an important liturgical function — guardian of the Temple gates — responsible for order and access to the house of God. His inclusion in these genealogical lists indicates his stable status within the restored Levitical community.

sens: The prophet author of the book of Abdias, fourth among the twelve minor prophets
H5662L.detail: 1. Abdias is the name of the fourth prophet of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament. His book prophesies against Edom, the enemy kingdom of Judah. Almost nothing is known about his personal life, but it is likely that he lived during the time of the great prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, during or after the exile of Judah (around the 6th century BC). His short but intense message carries a divine judgment against Edom for its pride and cruelty towards Judah.
H5662L.origine: The name Abdias means "servant of Jehovah" in Hebrew. It comes from the root "ebed" (servant) and the divine name "Yah" (Jehovah). This name was borne by several important characters in the history of Israel, from the time of the divided monarchy to the period of the temple reconstruction.
H5662L.emploi: Several men bore the name Abdias in the Old Testament: a military chief under David (1 Chronicles 12:9), a supervisor of the restoration work of the temple under King Josiah, the steward of King Ahab who hid more than a hundred prophets during the persecution of Jezebel, and others (princes, Levites, priests, gatekeepers). But the most famous is the prophet author of the book that bears his name, fourth of the twelve minor prophets, who delivered a divine message to the people of Judah regarding the judgment on Edom.
H5662L.portee: The book of Abdias reminds us that God judges the nations that mistreat His people and that He does not tolerate pride. It is a call to trust in God even when enemies seem powerful, and a promise that the Lord protects and defends those who belong to Him.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Zebulun during the time of King David
The most famous: minor prophet whose book speaks against Edom
Chief of the household of King Ahab who hid prophets during Jezebel's persecution
Other characters bearing this name in the history of Israel
H5662M.detail: 1. In 1 Chronicles 27:19, Obadiah (Jischemaeja) is the father of a leader of the twelve tribes of Zebulun during the time of King David. 2. The prophet Obadiah is the author of the fourth book of the twelve minor prophets; he likely lived during the time of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, and his book pronounces judgments against Edom. 3. Under King Ahab, there was an Obadiah who directed the royal household and who, at the risk of his life, hid more than a hundred prophets to save them from Jezebel's persecution. 4. Scripture mentions at least thirteen people bearing this name: Levites, tribal leaders, priests, porters, and descendants of David, demonstrating its widespread use in the history of Israel.
H5662M.origine: The name Obadiah comes from Hebrew meaning "servant of Jehovah" or "servant of the Lord." This name reflects the piety characteristic of the people of Israel, who saw themselves as serving the living God. Several important figures in biblical history bore this name, showing its spiritual prestige.
H5662M.emploi: Obadiah is best known as the author of the prophetic book that bears his name in the biblical canon. In 1 Chronicles 27:19, he is mentioned as the father of Jischemaeja, leader of the tribe of Zebulun. However, the history of Israel counted at least thirteen Obadiahs: Levites involved in the restoration of the temple under Josiah, an officer in Ahab's palace who protected the prophets, descendants of David, and participants in the restoration of the people after the exile. Thus, this name regularly reappears in Israel, from the time of David to the era of Nehemiah.
H5662M.portee: The name Obadiah reminds us that the service of the Lord has always characterized the people of God. The figure of the prophet Obadiah shows that the Lord communicates His word even in times of apostasy and persecution. The Obadiah who hid the prophets under Ahab illustrates that the fear of God can lead to acts of courage and justice, even in the face of the most hostile human power.

sens: Prince of Judah sent on a teaching mission by King Jehoshaphat
H5662N.detail: Obadiah is a chief of Judah chosen by King Jehoshaphat to teach in the cities of the kingdom. He appears only once in the Bible, mentioned alongside other leaders (Ben-Haïl, Zechariah, Nethaneel, and Micah) during this educational and religious mission launched in the third year of Jehoshaphat's reign (2 Chronicles 17:7). His name means "servant of the Lord" in Hebrew, suggesting a man devoted to divine service.
H5662N.origine: The name Obadiah comes from two Hebrew words: "ebed" (servant) and "Yah" (short form of the Lord's name). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing an individual's relationship with God. The Bible mentions several characters bearing this name, the most famous being the prophet Obadiah, author of the shortest book in the Old Testament; but this one is distinct and belongs to the time of Jehoshaphat.
H5662N.emploi: Obadiah is mentioned only once, in 2 Chronicles 17:7, as one of the ten princes that King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent on an official teaching mission in the cities of the kingdom in the 9th century B.C. This mention places him in an important administrative and religious role: he was part of the governing elite and participated in a significant religious reform. The context indicates that it was a royal initiative to strengthen the knowledge of God among the people.
H5662N.portee: This brief mention shows us how the faithful kings of Judah relied on trustworthy men to spread religious teaching. It illustrates the importance that the Bible attributes to instructing the people in faith, and how God used government leaders to support this work.

sens: Levite supervisor of the restoration work of the temple under King Josiah
Servant of Jehovah (meaning of the name)
H5662O.detail:
1. Obadiah is a Levite from the family of Merari who supervised the workers responsible for restoring the temple in Jerusalem during the time of King Josiah (2 Chronicles 34:12). His role was to ensure the quality and honesty of the work done during these important renovation efforts.
2. The name Obadiah literally means "servant of Jehovah" (from Hebrew "servant" and the divine name). It is a common name in the Old Testament, borne by several characters faithful to God.
H5662O.origine: The Hebrew name Obadiah (עֹבַדְיָהוּ) is composed of two elements: the word meaning "servant, one who serves" and the divine name "Yah" (Jehovah). It expresses the idea of a life dedicated to the service of God. This name was particularly given to Levites and temple servants, and several characters in the Old Testament bore it, including the prophet Obadiah who prophesied against Edom.
H5662O.emploi: Obadiah appears only once in the Bible in 2 Chronicles 34:12, where he is mentioned as a Levite from the family of Merari. At that time (under the reign of Josiah), the temple in Jerusalem needed significant repairs. Obadiah and other Levites were given the responsibility of supervising the workers and ensuring that the work was done with integrity. His role demonstrates the importance of the Levites in organizing and managing the affairs of the temple.
H5662O.portee: The character of Obadiah illustrates the role of the Levites as servants of God in the temple. His commitment to the restoration of the sanctuary reflects the spiritual priority given to maintaining the house of God. For today's believer, this name reminds us that serving God can be expressed in concrete tasks, carried out with integrity and faithfulness.

sens: Priest and head of a family who returned from exile with Ezra
Man whose name means "servant of the Lord"
H5662P.detail:
1. Obadiah is a priest from the family of Joab who, upon returning from Babylonian exile, accompanies the scribe Ezra to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:9). He brings with him two hundred eighteen men from his household, demonstrating the importance of his family. His Hebrew name literally means "servant of the Lord," a pious name that reflects the piety of the priestly families of Israel.
2. Beyond this passage, several men bore this same name in the history of Israel: a minor prophet whose book prophesies against Edom, a courageous officer of King Ahab who hid more than a hundred prophets during Jezebel's persecution, and other leaders and servants of worship. Each embodied dedication to the service of God in their generation.
H5662P.origine: The name Obadiah comes from Hebrew "ebed" (servant) and "Yah" (short form of the name of God, the Lord). It is a theophoric name—composed of the divine name—very common among Israelites to express dedication to God. The same root "ebed" appears in many biblical proper names and in the ordinary word designating servant or slave.
H5662P.emploi: Obadiah is mentioned only once in this passage of Ezra 8:9, where he appears as one of the heads of priestly houses who organize the return of the exiles. His role is administrative and religious: he gathers his own and brings them back to Jerusalem. The fact that he is named with a specific number of companions (two hundred eighteen) underscores his importance in the reconstitution of the post-exilic community.
H5662P.portee: This character reminds us that the return from exile was not an anonymous event of masses: specific families, led by faithful and responsible men, rebuilt Israel. Obadiah embodies the model of the pious leader who gathers his own and brings them back to the house of God—an encouraging image for any community in reconstruction.

sens: Minor prophet of the people of Israel
Man of high status bearing this name at various times in Israel's history
H5662Q.detail: 1. Obadiah is best known as the 4th minor prophet of the Bible. Nothing is known about his personal life, but he likely lived during the time of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. His prophetic book pronounces judgments against Edom, the neighboring people of Israel. 2. The name Obadiah also refers to several other important figures in Israel's history: a chief of the Levites who oversaw the restoration of the temple under King Josiah; an administrator of King Ahab's house who risked his life by hiding over 100 prophets during Jezebel's persecution; a prince of Judah under King Jehoshaphat; and others. Nehemiah 10:5 mentions an Obadiah among those who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah after the exile.
H5662Q.origine: The Hebrew name עֹבַדְיָהוּ literally means "servant of Jehovah" (obad = servant, yah = Jehovah). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name and expresses a relationship of allegiance to God. Many important figures in Israel have borne this name throughout the centuries.
H5662Q.emploi: The name Obadiah is held by at least 13 different people in the Bible, reflecting its importance and popularity. The primary source is the minor prophet whose book is one of the 12 minor prophecies; he prophesies against Edom and its fate. Other Obadiahs hold positions of responsibility: chief of the Levites, royal administrator, prince, priest, or man sealing covenants. The mention in Nehemiah 10:5 places an Obadiah among the leaders who solemnly commit to uphold the Law after the return from exile in Babylon.

sens: Prophet of Israel during the Exile and the return
H5662R.detail: Obadiah is the name of a prophet whose book consists of only one chapter in the Bible. This prophet was tasked with pronouncing a word of judgment against Edom, Israel's cousin country. His name literally means "servant of the Lord," which summarizes his vocation: to be the spokesperson for the God of Israel to announce His judgment (Obadiah 1:1).
H5662R.origine: The name Obadiah comes from two Hebrew words: "Abad" (to serve) and "Yah" (God, a short form of the divine name). It expresses the prophet's relationship to God: he is the servant, the instrument through which God speaks. Several men bore this name in Israel's history, but the most well-known remains the prophet whose book bears the name.
H5662R.emploi: Obadiah is mentioned only once by his full name in the Bible: at the beginning of the book that bears his name (Obadiah 1:1). This prophetic book, though short, contains an important message: God's judgment against Edom for its pride and enmity towards Judah. The context suggests that Obadiah prophesied during the Exile or shortly thereafter, likely during the time of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, although the details of his life remain largely unknown. His message remains a call to recognize God's justice towards the nations that oppose His people.
H5662R.portee: Obadiah teaches the reader that God uses even lesser-known prophets to announce His judgments on the nations. His name reminds us that every authentic prophet is merely a servant of God, tasked with faithfully conveying His word. This small book also shows that God's judgment against pride and violence is never without effect, even when the voice announcing it seems solitary.

sens: Ethiopian eunuch in the service of King Zedekiah
Man who freed the prophet Jeremiah from prison
H5663.detail: Ebed-Melech is an Ethiopian eunuch who served in the court of King Zedekiah of Judah during the siege of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. His name literally means "servant of the king." When the prophet Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern by the princes of Judah (Jeremiah 38:7), Ebed-Melech learned of this unjust act. Moved by compassion, he approached the king and interceded for the prophet, obtaining permission to rescue him. He then organized a rescue: he took thirty men with him (Jeremiah 38:10) and descended to the cistern, where he provided worn rags and old clothes to protect Jeremiah from the ropes (Jeremiah 38:12), thus showing kindness to the prisoner. His act of justice towards Jeremiah made him an instrument of God: he received a word from the Lord through Jeremiah, promising that his life would be spared during the fall of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:16).
H5663.origine: His Hebrew name עֶ֫בֶד מֶ֫לֶךְ (Ebed-Melech) means "servant of the king" (עֶ֫בֶד "servant, slave" and מֶ֫לֶךְ "king"). Although he is a servant in the literal sense — a eunuch in the service of the royal court — his name also becomes a description of his social condition and role with the sovereign.
H5663.emploi: Ebed-Melech appears only in the book of Jeremiah, in chapters 38-39, during the final siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar (around 588 B.C.). He is mentioned six times, always in connection with the rescue of Jeremiah: first as the one who discovers the prophet's imprisonment and intervenes with the king (Jeremiah 38:7-8), then as the one who organizes and executes the rescue with compassion (Jeremiah 38:10-12). He finally appears as the recipient of a prophetic promise of personal deliverance (Jeremiah 39:16).
H5663.portee: Ebed-Melech embodies the virtues of compassion and justice: although a mere servant and foreigner in a royal court, he dares to defend a man unjustly oppressed and acts at the risk of his own position. His story shows that God notices and rewards those who stand for truth and mercy, regardless of their social status or origins. It also reveals God's faithfulness to those who honor His messengers.

sens: One of Daniel's three friends in Babylon, whose Babylonian name means 'servant of Nebo'
Young Jewish man deported under Nebuchadnezzar, renamed by the chief of the palace eunuchs
One of the three companions refusing to defile themselves with the king's royal food
One of the three thrown into the fiery furnace and miraculously saved
H5664.detail:
1. Abed-Nego is one of the four young Jews of royal or noble blood (along with Daniel, Hananiah, and Mishael) whom Nebuchadnezzar brought to Babylon during the exile. His original Hebrew name is Azariah, but the chief of the king's eunuchs renames him "Abed-Nego," a Babylonian name that literally means "servant of Nebo" (Nebo being a Babylonian deity).
2. Along with his three companions, Abed-Nego refuses to defile himself by eating the king's food, which would contradict the dietary laws given by God to the Israelites: he asks the chief of the eunuchs to allow them to eat vegetables and drink water, and God makes them stronger than all who eat at the king's table.
3. Abed-Nego is among the three men thrown into the fiery furnace for refusing to bow down to the golden statue that Nebuchadnezzar erected: they are miraculously protected by an angel and emerge unharmed from the flames, leading the king to acknowledge the power of the God of Israel.
H5664.origine: The name Abed-Nego is a Babylonian composition: "abed" means "servant" and "Nego" refers to Nebo, the Babylonian god of knowledge and writing. It is a name imposed by foreign authority, marking the Babylonian regime's intention to strip the young Jews of their religious identity. His original name, Azariah, means in Hebrew "the Lord helps."
H5664.emploi: Abed-Nego is mentioned upon his arrival in Babylon in Daniel 1:7, where the chief of the eunuchs confers upon him his new Babylonian name. He is one of the four young men from the Judean elite taken captive. Along with his companions, he becomes a model of faithfulness to God's laws despite the pressures of King Nebuchadnezzar's palace. His story illustrates how to remain faithful to one's faith in a foreign land, refuse religious compromises (impure food, idolatry), and trust in God's power.
H5664.portee: The story of Abed-Nego teaches the Christian reader that remaining faithful to God in a hostile environment is possible and that God honors those who refuse compromises, even in the face of the most overwhelming political power. It shows that the change of name and culture imposed by a foreign regime cannot strip the believer of their true spiritual identity. It invites a resolute obedience to God's principles rather than to human authority, and affirms that God delivers those who trust Him.

sens: One of the three Jewish companions of Daniel in exile in Babylon
Young man renamed by King Nebuchadnezzar during his deportation
Faithful friend who refused to defile himself by eating royal food
Courageous martyr thrown into the fiery furnace for his refusal to worship an idol
H5665.detail:
1. Abed-Nego is one of the three young Jews deported to Babylon under King Nebuchadnezzar, along with Shadrach and Meshach, faithful companions of the prophet Daniel. He first appears in Daniel 1:6, where he is originally called Azaria before being renamed by King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:49).
2. This young man categorically refuses to violate God's Law by eating royal food that would have tainted his ritual purity. This obedience to divine commandments, even far from his homeland, shows his spiritual determination from the very beginning of his exile.
3. When the king orders all the inhabitants to bow down before a golden statue, Abed-Nego and his two friends courageously refuse (Daniel 3:12-16), declaring to the king: "We do not need to give you an answer concerning this" (Daniel 3:16). They know that this idolatry would betray their God.
4. For this insubordination, Abed-Nego is thrown into a furnace "heated seven times more" (Daniel 3:20, 3:23). Miraculously, an angel of the Lord protects them, and the three men come out unharmed from the furnace (Daniel 3:28), which leads the king himself to bless the God who saves His servants.
H5665.origine: The Aramaic name "Abed-Nego" means "servant of Nebo," Nebo being a Babylonian deity. It is the name given by King Nebuchadnezzar to replace the Jewish name Azaria, "Yahweh helps." This name change was part of the Babylonian re-education policy for the young exiles from the Jewish elite. Despite this imposed renaming, the young man remained faithful to the God of Israel and maintained his spiritual identity.
H5665.emploi: Abed-Nego appears in the book of Daniel at the time of the deportation in 605 B.C. His story plays a major role in Daniel 2 and 3, particularly during the crisis of the idolatry of the golden statue. Along with his companions Shadrach and Meshach, he symbolizes Jewish faithfulness despite the political and religious pressure of the Babylonian regime. His courage in the face of death and his miraculous deliverance in Daniel 3:28-29 serve as a powerful testimony to the power of the God of Israel, prompting the king himself to acknowledge him and reinstate him in his responsibilities (Daniel 3:29-30). The story of Abed-Nego illustrates how remaining faithful to God in exile leads to supernatural liberation and honor.
H5665.portee: Abed-Nego represents for the believer a model of faithfulness to God in the midst of an idolatrous and hostile world. His refusal to compromise his faith, even in the face of the threat of death, teaches that obedience to God is better than conformity to the world. His story reminds the reader that God never abandons them, even when they seem alone, and that sincere trust in Him can lead to miraculous deliverance and a powerful testimony to those around us.

sens: Having great thickness, a large physical dimension
Having a lot of flesh, corpulent
Having become fat, heavy-bodied
Figuratively: becoming insensitive, forgetful of one's duties
H5666.detail:
1. The word primarily describes something of great dimension or physical thickness: when Rehoboam states, "My little finger is thicker than my father's loins" (1 Kings 12:10), he means that his little finger surpasses in thickness the largest part of his father's body — it is an image of increased power.
2. The word applies to a person who has become fat and fleshy, someone who has gained weight: the Segond translates this state of excess flesh as "plump."
3. When the Bible says that Israel "became fat" (Deuteronomy 32:15), it describes a people who have become materially prosperous, living in abundance and physical satisfaction.
4. This physical abundance also marks a thickening of moral insensitivity: Israel, having become fat and satisfied, "kicked" and revolted against God, forgetting the one who had nourished them. The word thus evokes the hardening of the heart that follows the forgetfulness of God.
H5666.origine: The Hebrew root עבה expresses the idea of thickness and density: what is thick, dense, taking up space. The word appears rarely in the Old Testament (only three occurrences), always in the concrete or figurative sense of what has become heavy, cumbersome, insensitive. The family of the word includes derivatives related to thickness and weight.
H5666.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Segond, always in the form "has become" or "have become." In Deuteronomy 32:15, Moses reproaches Israel for having become fat — physically nourished but spiritually ungrateful — and thus having forgotten their God. In 1 Kings 12:10 and 2 Chronicles 10:10, the young king Rehoboam uses the word in the comparative to boast of his superhuman strength against the people: his little finger would be thicker, and thus stronger, than the loins (the seat of strength) of his father Solomon. In all cases, the term signals a physical reality (obesity, thickness) that carries a moral or political significance.
H5666.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the danger of material abundance: when God's blessings multiply, there is a great risk of forgetting the one who gives them and becoming insensitive to His voice. Fat Israel serves as a warning: prosperity, far from distancing one from God, can thicken the heart and close the ears to His word. It is a call to remain vigilant in abundance.

sens: object given as security for a debt
clothing or personal property seized as collateral
return of this property to the creditor
H5667.detail:
1. A pledge is an object that a borrower gives to their creditor to guarantee that they will repay their debt. It is a form of material guarantee: if the loan is not repaid, the creditor keeps the object as compensation (Deuteronomy 24:10-11).
2. The pledge often refers to clothing or personal property that is seized when someone cannot pay: it is a means of forcing repayment. The law protects the one who must return the pledge — even if they are poor, it should not be kept overnight, as it may be their only garment for sleeping (Deuteronomy 24:12).
3. The verb "to retain a pledge" refers to the action of confiscating or keeping this object while awaiting repayment, which is subject to strict rules of justice.
H5667.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to engage" or "to bind." It expresses the idea of something that holds two parties together — a link between the creditor and the debtor. In the legal practice of the Old Testament, the pledge is the instrument that guarantees the fulfillment of the contractual obligation.
H5667.emploi: The word appears four times in Deuteronomy 24, a passage that legislates the rights of the poor. The law establishes strict protections: one cannot enter someone's house to take a pledge (24:10); the creditor must stay outside and wait for the debtor to bring it to them (24:11); if the debtor is poor, their pledge must be returned every evening, as it may be their garment (24:12-13). This usage shows that the pledge, although legal, must be exercised with compassion towards the poor.
H5667.portee: This law reveals God's heart for social justice: even in commercial relationships, the dignity and basic needs of the poor must be respected. The creditor who returns the pledge at sunset performs an act of justice that pleases the Lord (24:13). It is a call for Christians to temper legal demands with mercy.

sens: As a result of something, due to something
In view of, to achieve a result
So that, in order to
H5668.detail:
1. The primary meaning is causal: something happens or is desired because another cause provokes or explains it. "The ground will be cursed because of you" (Genesis 3:17) means that Adam's disobedience is the reason for the curse on the ground. This word connects two facts: one explains or justifies the other.
2. The second meaning is intentional or instrumental: an action is undertaken not for itself, but to achieve a goal or serve another purpose. "Is it not to recognize and explore the city" (2 Samuel 10:3): David's messengers come to explore, which is their hidden objective. The goal precedes and justifies the action.
3. Finally, the word can introduce a consequence or an expected result, almost marking a finality. "In this way, you will dwell in the land of Goshen" (Genesis 46:34): by responding this way, Jacob's sons act with the intention of obtaining this permission. The causal link is tinged with intentionality.
H5668.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root meaning to pass, to cross (עָבַר). The basic idea is that of a passage or a crossing: one surpasses a point to arrive at a consequence. That is why "because of" carries the sense of a reason that causes a transition from one state to another. This root is found in many Hebrew words; here, it has been grammaticalized into a preposition and conjunction to express causality and purpose.
H5668.emploi: This word appears 47 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis, Exodus, the books of Samuel, and the Psalms. It is almost always used to connect a cause or reason to a consequence or goal. In Genesis 18:26-32, Abraham intercedes for Sodom "because of" the righteous who are there: their presence justifies forgiveness. In 1 Samuel 12:22, God refuses to abandon Israel "because of" His great name: His divine reputation is the reason for His faithfulness. In 2 Samuel 10:3, David is suspected "to" recognize the city: exploration is the true hidden motive. The word thus plays on causality in a broad sense: factual reason, moral justification, or desired goal.
H5668.portee: This word helps the reader understand divine and human logic: what motives, what reasons drive God or people to act? It invites one to see that nothing happens by chance, but that there is always a cause and an intention. For the Christian life, this reminds us that our actions have reasons and consequences, that God acts based on motives (His love, His glory, His faithfulness), and that we can plead based on His reasons for acting.

sens: cultivated grain that is ground to make bread
harvest, production of the land
H5669.detail:
1. Wheat is the grain of cereal that the Israelites began to eat upon their arrival in the Promised Land. In Joshua 5:11, after the Passover at Gilgal, they eat for the first time "the wheat of the land": these are the ripe ears that they can roast or grind into flour to make bread. It is the daily food that replaces the manna of the desert.
2. By extension, the word refers to the harvest, the crop, everything that the land produces. In Joshua 5:12, when "the manna ceased," it is because the children of Israel "ate the produce of the land of Canaan": wheat here symbolizes the new abundance that God gives them as an inheritance, instead of the miraculous bread of the desert.
H5669.origine: The Hebrew word חִטָּה (chittah) comes from a root that evokes what is produced, harvested, drawn from the earth. It is part of the vocabulary of plowing and harvesting. It is a concrete agricultural product, the visible wealth of the land of Canaan.
H5669.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Joshua 5, at the decisive moment when Israel leaves the desert and begins to live off the fruits of its Promised Land. The two verses recount the same event: the end of divine manna and the beginning of ordinary sustenance, through wheat and the products of the conquered land. It is a moment of transition, where the miracle of the desert gives way to the normal order of agricultural life.
H5669.portee: This passage shows that entering the Promised Land signifies not only a military victory but also access to a new life, nourished by the work and the land that God gives as an inheritance. Wheat, stable food and fruit of the soil, symbolizes God's concrete blessing: He moves from miraculous sustenance to the gift of fertile land. For the believer, it is a reminder that God provides not through extraordinary eternal signs, but by giving work and a land to take root in.

sens: To give money or goods to someone, with the expectation that they will be repaid
To borrow money or goods from someone
To retain or seize something as collateral for a debt
To deviate from one's path or direction
H5670.detail:
1. To lend means to make a sum of money or goods available to someone, with the expectation that they will return it. It is an act of generosity inscribed in the law of Israel: in Deuteronomy 15:8, the Lord commands to open one's hand and lend to the poor to meet their needs, without refusal or selfish calculation.
2. To borrow is the inverse action: to receive from someone a sum or goods that one commits to return. In Deuteronomy 15:6, the blessed people of God "will not borrow" from the nations, for they will live in abundance and independence.
3. To seize a pledge means to retain an object belonging to the debtor as collateral that the debt will be paid. The Law in Deuteronomy 24:10 protects the poor by prohibiting the creditor from entering their house to take the pledge: they must wait outside for the debtor to bring it to them.
4. To deviate from one's path means to stray, to turn away from one's way. In Joel 2:7, the locusts do not deviate from their path, meaning they move straight ahead, without changing direction.
H5670.origine: The Hebrew word עָבַט (avat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of taking or seizing. Its primary meaning is probably "to give as a pledge" or "to take as a pledge," hence the idea of credit and exchange: the one who lends "seizes" a promise of repayment, the one who borrows "gives" their word or an object as collateral. The meaning of "to deviate" in Joel 2:7 derives from this image of "taking" or "turning away" from its natural course.
H5670.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in contexts of law and social morality. In Deuteronomy 15, it states Israel's obligation to lend to the poor: it is a mark of divine blessing to be able to give credit to other nations without needing it oneself. In Deuteronomy 24, the same law protects the poor debtor by regulating how the creditor can seize the pledge. In Joel 2:7, the word takes on a completely different meaning, applied to locusts that advance in formation without turning: here, "to deviate" means "to leave" or "to stray." This diversity shows that the verb covers the general idea of giving, retaining, and diverting.
H5670.portee: This word reminds the Christian that lending is not merely a transactional act, but a moral command rooted in divine law. Generosity towards the poor and respect for their dignity must go hand in hand: one lends freely, but does not violate the privacy or rights of the borrower. It is a call to reflect God's generosity towards us.

sens: obligation to repay a sum of money or return an item
heavy burden imposed on someone
moral or religious burden
H5671.detail:
1. A debt is primarily a sum of money or an item that one owes to someone else and is obligated to repay or return. It is a legal and concrete obligation.
2. The word also evokes a heavy burden that weighs on the debtor: like a load one carries that crushes, a mass that accumulates and becomes unbearable. In Habakkuk 2:6, the prophet denounces one who "increases the burden of his debts," showing that debts add up until they become an oppressive weight.
3. In a moral and religious sense, a debt is an obligation to someone, a wrongdoing to be repaired: the notion of debt can express what one owes morally or what is religiously incumbent upon them.
H5671.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of weight, burden, that which presses heavily. This is why the Bible speaks of "debts" as a burden: a debt is never light; it always weighs on the one who bears it. In New Testament Greek, the word "opheilêma" (ὀφείλημα) also translates this concept of debt, and the Lord teaches us to ask for forgiveness of "our debts" as well as our sins (Matthew 6:12).
H5671.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Habakkuk 2:6. The prophet Habakkuk addresses the oppressors who enrich themselves by stripping others, burdening them with crushing debts. The image of the burden of debts that accumulates symbolizes economic injustice and exploitation: those who accumulate what does not belong to them end up being overwhelmed by their own crimes. Thus, debt becomes a biblical image of iniquity that weighs on the guilty.
H5671.portee: This word teaches us that debts—whether financial or moral—are never neutral: they weigh, they oppress, they demand to be settled. For the Christian, this reminds us of the importance of integrity in business, and also that the forgiveness of debts (remission) is an act of grace. Habakkuk warns us that those who enrich themselves through injustice and burden others with debts will sooner or later see that burden fall back upon them.

sens: Measurable dimension of an object, from surface to core
Massive or bulging part of something
Density or depth of a surface
H5672.detail:
1. Thickness is the measured distance from one side to the other of an object, perpendicular to its surface. In 1 Kings 7:26, the word describes the thickness of the molten sea: "Its thickness was a handbreadth"—referring to the wall of the basin, which had the depth of a hand's width. It is a concrete measure of material.
2. The word can also refer to something massive or dense—the "thick backs of their shields" in Job 15:26 evokes a robust protection, the prominent and solidly thick part. Here, thickness speaks of strength or solidity.
3. In Jeremiah 52:21, the column of the temple had a "thickness" of four fingers, a physical measure of the wall. The architectural context shows that this word measures the space occupied by the material itself, from hollow to filled.
H5672.origine: The word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be thick" or "to thicken." It denotes the quality of that which is not thin or hollow, but has substance and depth. The family of this word in Hebrew carries this idea of fullness and material density.
H5672.emploi: The word appears about five times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the architectural descriptions of the temple and its objects. In 1 Kings 7:26 and 2 Chronicles 4:5, it measures the wall of the large bronze basin. In Jeremiah 52:21, it indicates the thickness of the sacred columns during the destruction of the temple. Once, in Job 15:26, it is used figuratively to evoke the massive solidity of shields. The context remains always technical and material.
H5672.portee: This word reminds us that in the tabernacle and the temple, every detail was thought out and measured: the exact proportions of the worship objects manifested the order and beauty of God's plan. For the believer, it is a call to notice how God pays attention to details, even the smallest, in His work.

sens: Activity of construction or manufacturing, physical work
Administrative task, management of a province or a charge
Service rendered, function regularly performed
Religious service, worship offered to God
H5673.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes concrete, physical work: it refers to the construction activity of God's house in Jerusalem. In Ezra 4:24, we speak of the "work" of the house that stops and resumes; in Ezra 5:8, the "work" advances quickly.
2. It can signify an administrative charge, the responsibility of managing a territory or an official function. Daniel and his companions receive the "stewardship" of the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:49, 3:12), meaning the leadership and management of that region.
3. The word applies to any regular activity of execution and service, whether material or administrative.
4. It also designates religious service: in Ezra 6:18, we refer to the "service" of God performed by the priests and Levites according to ancient prescriptions.
H5673.origine: This Hebrew word expresses the general idea of work and activity. Its root refers to effort and action. The word belongs to the common vocabulary of the Old Testament and regularly appears to describe both material tasks and official functions or worship rendered to God.
H5673.emploi: The word appears six times, almost always in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which recount the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple. It is used for the construction work of the Temple (Ezra 4:24; 5:8; 6:7), for the royal administration entrusted to Daniel and his friends (Daniel 2:49; 3:12), and for the religious service of the Temple (Ezra 6:18). The meaning varies according to the context: material work, administrative management, or sacred service.
H5673.portee: This word reminds the reader that all honest work, whether manual, administrative, or religious, has dignity. In the context of the return from exile, it shows how the Jews, under royal protection, set about rebuilding and serving God. It invites the Christian to see their own work not as something contemptible, but as a legitimate activity: whether it serves to build, to manage, or to honor God.

sens: Traverser un lieu, un espace, d'un côté à l'autre
Dépasser, laisser derrière soi en allant plus loin
Aller le long de, longer, parcourir
Disparaître, cesser d'exister, prendre fin
Transgresser un ordre, une limite établie
Laisser aller, permettre de continuer
H5674A.detail:
1. To cross a place, a space, from one side to the other: the most concrete and fundamental meaning. To cross a physical boundary, a watercourse, or a region. In Genesis 32:22-23, Jacob "crossed" the ford of the Jabbok with his family: this is the simple and straightforward crossing. Similarly, in Deuteronomy 2:29, permission is requested to "cross" the Jordan to enter Canaan. Imagine someone crossing a river or walking through a land: this is where the word begins.
2. To surpass, to leave behind while going further: when one passes something, one leaves it to the side. In 2 Samuel 19:39, the people and the king "crossed" the Jordan together — they do not stop there, they continue beyond.
3. To go along, to follow, to traverse: to cross by walking, often quickly. In Genesis 12:6, Abram "passed" through the place of Shechem: he travels through the land.
4. To disappear, to cease to exist, to come to an end: when something "passes," it goes away and is no more. The waves that "pass" over us (Psalm 42:8) overwhelm us and then leave us. It is the passage of time, the erasure.
5. To transgress an order, an established limit: to go beyond what is forbidden. This is the secret link between physically crossing and violating a rule: one "passes" the barrier that should have been respected.
6. To let go, to allow to continue: in certain contexts, to let someone pass means to allow them to go on their way without stopping them. This is the causative sense: one helps to cross, one tolerates the passage.
H5674A.origine: The verb עָבַר (avar) is a pure root of Hebrew with the fundamental meaning "to go beyond, to cross." Its starting image is that of physical movement beyond a limit. The same root is found in Aramaic with the same meaning. Several words from the same family retain this idea: עֵבֶר (éver, "beyond, region on the other side"), עִבְרִי (ivri, "Hebrew," one who comes "from the other side of the river"), עַבְרָה (avra, "passage"). The central notion is always the crossing of a boundary, physical or moral.
H5674A.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (441 occurrences), very dense in the Pentateuch and in the Historical Books. It primarily describes concrete crossings: Noah "passed" a wind (Genesis 8:1) to dry the earth, the fathers crossed the Jordan (very repeated in Deuteronomy 2), the Israelites crossed the Red Sea and the river (Numbers 33:8). But the word expands: it means to travel (Genesis 30:32, the flocks that "pass"), to let pass (Exodus 12:23, the angel who ignores the marked houses), and also to transgress or abolish a law (Numbers 5:14, jealousy that "passes" over someone). The context determines whether it is simple crossing or infringement. In poetry (Psalms 42:8, Jeremiah 23:9), the word takes on a shade of overwhelming or invading.
H5674A.portee: This word teaches the believer that life is a passage: we traverse this world without remaining in it. But above all, it reminds us that a boundary crossed can be a transgression if it violates God's order. The orders that forbid "passing" certain territories (Deuteronomy 2:4-5, Deuteronomy 2:37) show that God sets boundaries. The verb invites us to discern between permitted passage and forbidden transgression, between legitimate movement and exceeding limits.

sens: Éprouver une vive contrariété, une montée de colère
Se montrer irrité, manifestant son déplaisir par son attitude ou ses actes
Être provoqué à la colère par quelqu'un ou quelque chose
H5674B.detail:
1. To become irritated means to experience a strong displeasure that rises within like a heat. This is what the Lord feels when Moses begs Him to enter Canaan: "the Lord was angry with me because of you" (Deuteronomy 3:26), His patience is exhausted and His anger ignites.
2. To be irritated means to manifest displeasure through concrete actions. God "was angry; a fire was kindled against Jacob" (Psalms 78:21) — His irritation does not remain hidden, it unfolds in action. Or again: "He greatly rejected Israel" (Psalms 78:59), thus showing that He was irritated.
3. To be irritated against someone means to be provoked to anger by their actions or words. He who "irritates" the king "sins against himself" (Proverbs 20:2), for the king's anger is dangerous — like the roar of a lion.
H5674B.origine: This Hebrew root fundamentally evokes the idea of burning, of inflaming internally. Irritation is a heat, a fervor that rises in the one who experiences it. It often figures in the Bible as God's passionate anger in response to the unfaithfulness or insolence of His people.
H5674B.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and the wisdom books. It regularly describes the Lord's anger towards Israel: irritated by ingratitude, sin, or the unfaithfulness of the people (Psalms 78:21, 78:59, 78:62; Deuteronomy 3:26; Psalms 89:39). It is also used for human anger: he who "irritates" the king exposes himself to retaliation (Proverbs 20:2). The word conveys an immediate and passionate reaction, different from a cold and calculated anger.
H5674B.portee: This word reminds us that God's irritation is never arbitrary: it responds to unfaithfulness or rebellion. At the same time, it invites the reader to take seriously the gravity of sin, as it can move God to irritation. For those who serve God, it is also a call not to "irritate" Him through doubt or disobedience, just as one does not lightly provoke the anger of a fearsome king.

sens: Crossing a space, crossing a boundary
Moving from one place to another, advancing
Going beyond, surpassing
Disappearing, ceasing to exist
Transferring, passing to someone else
Forgiving, removing, making disappear
H5674C.detail:
1. Crossing a space, crossing a boundary: the most concrete meaning. When Joshua commands the children of Israel to cross the Jordan, they must physically "pass" this river (Joshua 4:8). It is the movement of crossing a natural obstacle or a border.

2. Moving from one place to another, advancing: continuing on the path, walking forward. The Egyptian people "pass" from one city to another under Pharaoh's order (Genesis 47:21).

3. Going beyond, surpassing: leaving something behind, going further. The kingship "passes" from the house of Saul to that of David (2 Samuel 3:10): it changes hands.

4. Disappearing, ceasing to exist: the idea that something goes away and does not return. Asa "makes disappear" the abominations of the land (2 Chronicles 15:8); Job asks God to remove his sin from His eyes (Job 7:21).

5. Transferring, passing to someone else: giving to someone what one possessed. Haman's authority "passes" to Esther (Esther 8:2): she receives his position.

6. Forgiving, removing, making disappear: in the spiritual context, "passing" a sin means forgiving it and setting it aside. When David confesses his sin, God forgives him, makes it "pass" (2 Samuel 12:13).
H5674C.origine: The Hebrew verb עָבַר (abar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of crossing or traversing a space. It is a very common verb in the Hebrew Bible to describe physical movement. The word belongs to a broad Semitic family. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the idea of passing over, crossing a boundary, but also of forgiving or removing — hence the extension of meaning that goes from concrete movement to spiritual forgiveness.
H5674C.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the cited passages. It is first used in the literal sense: crossing a river (Joshua), crossing a border, transporting something from one place to another (2 Samuel 19:18 speaks of the boat that "transports" the king's household). It then takes on figurative and administrative meanings: kingship "passes" to someone else, meaning it changes ownership or holder (2 Samuel 3:10; Esther 8:2). It also extends to the moral and religious domain: orders or decrees "pass" (disappear), sins are "passed" or "forgiven." The context determines the exact meaning each time, but movement remains the central image: something or someone goes from one state or place to another.
H5674C.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reminds us that God can "make us pass" from one state to another: from sin to forgiveness, from slavery to freedom, from death to life. It also emphasizes that nothing lasts forever: abominations "pass," unjust decrees "pass," our sins can be "passed" — forgiven and removed. It is a word of liberation and hope: what crushes us can disappear, and we can move forward to a new stage of our journey with God.

sens: Crossing, traversing a physical boundary
Surpassing, leaving behind
Violating an order, a law, or a covenant
Becoming null, losing validity
Disappearing, ceasing to exist
H5674D.detail:
1. Crossing, traversing a physical boundary: the word first evokes the action of passing over or through an obstacle or boundary. It is the image of a person or an army crossing a river or climbing a hill.

2. Surpassing, leaving behind: the word also describes someone who surpasses another or who advances beyond a fixed point, like a thought that comes out of the mouth (Psalms 17:3).

3. Violating an order, a law, or a covenant: this is the most frequent meaning in the Bible. To transgress means to intentionally violate what has been commanded, like the Israelites who transgressed the covenant of the Lord (Joshua 23:16) or who refused to obey the voice of God (2 Kings 18:12).

4. Becoming null, losing validity: the word can also mean that a law or decree ceases to have force, becomes obsolete, or no longer applies.

5. Disappearing, ceasing to exist: the word finally expresses the idea that something fades away, vanishes, or completely ceases to be, like an enemy or a promise that disappears.
H5674D.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to pass" or "to cross." This basic image — crossing a boundary or an obstacle — naturally extends to the idea of exceeding the limits imposed by a law or commandment. The same root produces nouns and participles that describe one who passes, the passer, or the action of passing. It is a very ancient and common word in the Hebrew Bible, where it expresses both physical movement and moral violation.
H5674D.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the provided usages, concentrated mainly in the historical and prophetic books. In the majority of cases (14 translations as "transgress"), it designates the violation of a commandment or a covenant by the Israelites: Moses asks why they transgress the order of the Lord (Numbers 14:41), the Israelites transgressed the covenant (Joshua 23:16; 2 Kings 18:12), and the prophets accuse them of having broken the covenant with God (Hosea 6:7; Hosea 8:1; Isaiah 24:5). A few usages retain the more concrete sense of "passing" or "surpassing": a thought "comes out" of the mouth (Psalms 17:3), one "crosses" a threshold. The context reveals that this verb, even in the physical sense, often carries a nuance of infraction or breach of law. In Jeremiah 2:20, it describes a kind of servitude that is refused, which extends the idea of violation.
H5674D.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals that transgressing God — that is, violating His commandments or breaking His covenant — is not a distant moral weakness, but an active and conscious act of crossing the boundary He has set. The Bible shows that God takes every transgression seriously and that the consequences are grave. Understanding this word helps grasp the importance of obedience and the necessity of returning to God when we have exceeded His limits.

sens: to go from one side to the other, to cross a space
to overcome an obstacle or a limit
to exceed in quantity or importance
to flow, to disappear with time
H5674G.detail:
1. The verb "pass" describes the action of crossing, of going beyond: someone or something that moves from one place to another. In Ezekiel 39:11, "the valley of travelers" (literally "the valley of those who pass") refers to a valley through which one travels, where merchants and pilgrims pass. It is a transit valley, a path taken by caravans.
2. The word can also mean to cross a threshold or a point of no return: to pass a border, to cross a river, to venture beyond the known.
3. It can carry the sense of surpassing, going further or higher than the norm: to exceed a limit, to surpass a measure.
4. In a broader and more poetic sense, "pass" evokes the flight of time, the ephemeral: days pass, glory passes, all that is earthly flows and disappears.
H5674G.origine: The Hebrew root עָבַר (avar) is very ancient and expresses the fundamental movement of crossing. It evokes the concrete image of crossing a space: to ford a river, to cross a desert. The same root has given rise to other words in the semantic family: "Hebrew" (עִברִי, Ivri) literally means "one who has crossed," one who comes from the other side of the river. It is a very common word in the Old Testament, used for all types of passage.
H5674G.emploi: The verb "pass" (עָבַר) appears very frequently in the Hebrew Bible, in various contexts: crossing a sea or a river (like at the Red Sea), passing through a place during a journey, or figuratively, leaving behind a period of life. In the unique usage provided, Ezekiel 39:11, the participle "traveler" (one who passes) qualifies the valley: this place is defined by the fact that people pass through it, it is a valley of passage, of transit. The context speaks of the judgment of Gog and the place of his burial in Israel.
