H5674G.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of travel and change: we are all travelers on this earth, we cross stages, we leave behind what was. For the believer, this evokes the biblical idea that earthly life is a passage, a crossing towards eternity. Meditating on this verb invites us not to cling to things that pass, but to fix our gaze on what remains.

sens: to lack restraint and wisdom in the face of evil
to display excessive self-confidence
to despise warnings and limits
H5674H.detail:
1. To be arrogant means to act without prudent restraint, especially in the face of danger or evil. The arrogant rushes in without considering the consequences, unlike the wise who "turns away from evil" (Proverbs 14:16): he knows there are limits to respect.
2. It is to display an excessive confidence in oneself and in one's own strength. The arrogant believes he is immune to the traps and misfortunes that befall others, which makes him careless and dangerous to himself.
3. It is to refuse to listen, to fear God, or to acknowledge one's weaknesses. The passage in Proverbs contrasts the wise, prudent and aware of risks, with the foolish arrogant who rushes in headlong, certain that no harm will come to him.
H5674H.origine: The Hebrew word עָבַר (avar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of crossing, of exceeding a limit — in this case, that of prudence and respect. That is why "to be arrogant" literally means "to exceed the bounds": the arrogant ignores or despises the boundaries of wisdom and the fear of God. This meaning is found in other forms of the same word when they mean "to transgress" or "to violate."
H5674H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond, in Proverbs 14:16. It describes the attitude of one who believes he is above warnings and dangers: unlike the wise who seeks to avoid evil, the foolish arrogant exposes himself without fear, convinced that nothing can happen to him. The context of this proverb makes this clear: arrogance is a form of blindness to the realities of the world and divine justice.
H5674H.portee: This word warns us against pride and spiritual self-sufficiency. Arrogance makes us deaf to the counsel of wisdom and the warning signs that God places in our path. It is a serious trap for any Christian: to believe that one cannot fall, that one needs no one, that one understands better than others. The biblical entry reminds us that true wisdom begins with humility and the fear of God.

sens: region located on the other side of a river or border
administrative or political territory of a land divided by a geographical boundary
H5675.detail:
1. The word simply designates the region that extends beyond a river or a boundary. In Ezra, the context constantly speaks of the "side of the river," that is, the lands located on the other side of the great river (the Euphrates), in the region of Syria-Phoenicia and Palestine, under Persian rule. When one says "this side of the river" or "the other side of the river," it precisely designates a distinct region, separated by this natural boundary.
2. This word can also designate a province or an administrative territory as a region governed from a distant metropolis. In the royal letters addressed to the governors, the "side of the river" is an administrative district for which the governor reports to the king of Persia, with its treasury and its own political organization.
H5675.origine: The Aramaic word אֲבַר comes from the same root as the Hebrew עֵבֶר (éver), which means properly "side" or "bank." This root conveys the idea of crossing or passing beyond a limit. It is also found in the name "Hebrews," which perhaps originally designated the peoples "from the other side" of the Jordan or the great boundaries. In Aramaic of the first millennium, the term specialized to designate the administrative regions beyond the great rivers of the Persian Empire.
H5675.emploi: This Aramaic word appears exclusively in the book of Ezra (12 times), in sections containing official Persian documents. It always designates a region located on the other side of a river — in this case, the Euphrates. In these royal letters between the king of Persia and the local governors, the expression "side of the river" is a common administrative designation: it evokes both the natural barrier (the river) and the political region it delineates. The usages show that it is a bureaucratic term: we speak of the "tributes from the side of the river" (Ezra 4:20, 6:8), of the royal possession "from this side of the river" (Ezra 4:16), or of the "treasurers from the side of the river" (Ezra 7:21). The meaning remains constant: always a region, separated by a natural boundary, organized under Persian authority.
H5675.portee: This word reminds us how God governs His people through the structures and borders of the world of earthly empires. During the exile and return, the Jews are not independent political entities, but subjects living in provinces of a vast empire. Despite this condition, the text of Ezra shows that the Persian royal decrees ultimately allow for the reconstruction of the Temple. This geopolitical reality anchors the people's trust in the providence of God, who acts beyond political divisions and borders.

sens: the side of a thing, one of its edges or faces
the bank or edge of a river, sea
the region beyond or on this side of a natural boundary (river, mountain)
the place where something connects or applies to another thing
H5676G.detail:
1. The side of a thing refers to one of its faces or edges: thus in Exodus 28:26, the gold rings are placed "at the two ends of the breastplate, on the inner edge applied against the ephod" — this is the side by which one piece of fabric joins another.
2. The side of a river is its bank: in Numbers 32:19, the Israelites speak of possessing land "on this side of the Jordan" and "on the other side of the Jordan" to designate the two banks and the territories that depend on them.
3. A region beyond or on this side of a boundary refers to the territory located on one side or the other of a natural border: in Joshua 22:4, Moses gave the Reubenites and Gadites an inheritance "on the other side of the Jordan"; in Judges 11:18, they camp "beyond the Arnon," the river that marks the boundary of the territory of Moab.
4. The side by which something applies or connects to another: in 1 Kings 7:20, pomegranates adorn "the side of the lattice," meaning the bulge that adjoins the lattice.
H5676G.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to pass" or "to cross": one who crosses goes from one side to the other of a boundary. Hence comes the meaning of "region beyond," then by extension "side" or "edge" in general. The word is also used in Hebrew to mean "Hebrew" (one who comes from "the other side"), because Abraham crossed the Euphrates. This root evokes the idea of crossing from one bank to another.
H5676G.emploi: The word appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Joshua, Judges, and Samuel, where it serves to describe borders and territories. Its most frequent use concerns the Jordan: "the other side of the Jordan" (East of the Jordan where the Reubenites and Gadites live) contrasts with "this side" (West of the Jordan where the other tribes settle). The word can also refer to an edge or face of something: a piece of gold in Exodus, an ornament in 1 Kings, a steep mountain in 1 Samuel 14:4. In Jeremiah 48:28 and 49:32, "the side of a rock" or "the side of the desert" express a location. The context always clarifies whether it refers to a spatial side, a bank, or a region.
H5676G.portee: This word reminds us that land boundaries — rivers, mountains, lands — mark the history of God's people. It also emphasizes that God distributes territories with wisdom and justice: each tribe receives its inheritance on one side or the other of the Jordan according to the divine plan. For the Christian, this illustrates that God orders all things with a precise intention, including limits and separations.

sens: The other side of a geographical boundary (river, desert, mountain)
The opposite side of a space, in relation to where one stands
The region or territory located opposite
What stands on the other side, in front
H5676H.detail:
1. The other side of a geographical boundary: the word first designates the space that lies beyond a natural border. It typically refers to the other bank of the Jordan, which the Israelites speak of when they are about to conquer Canaan: "the Lord grant rest to your brothers as to you, and let them also possess the land that the Lord your God is giving them. Then you will return to take possession of the land that is your property… on this side of the Jordan" (Joshua 1:15). The river marks the boundary, and beyond it lies the promised land.
2. The opposite side of a space: the word can also simply refer to the side across, the other bank. When Gideon pursues Midian, the heads of the leaders are brought "to Gideon from the other side of the Jordan" (Judges 7:25) — that is, from the other bank in relation to this one.
3. The region or territory located opposite: in "on the other side of the Jordan, opposite Jericho" (Joshua 13:32), we see that beyond can designate an entire region. Here too, we speak of conquered regions "on the other side of the Jordan, from the torrent of the Arnon to the mountain of Hermon" (Deuteronomy 3:8).
4. What comes from the other side, what comes from in front: the wind can come "from the other side of the desert" (Job 1:19) — it blows from the region that lies beyond this desert.
H5676H.origine: The Hebrew word עֵבֶר (eber) comes from a root that evokes crossing, passage: something that is beyond, which must be crossed to reach. It is related to words meaning "to pass," "to cross." The word naturally designates what is on the other side of a barrier — river, mountain, desert — and one who lives beyond becomes a "Hebrew," a "passer" or one who comes from the other side. This etymology shows that for the ancient Israelites, the beyond was primarily thought of as a region reached by crossing a boundary.
H5676H.emploi: The word appears 55 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and in the narratives of the Pentateuch. It is used almost exclusively to designate a region beyond the Jordan — particularly the territories of the Amorites, Ammon, or Moab that the Israelites conquer or speak of. More broadly, it also describes the sides of any space: the flanks of a celestial chariot in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:9), one side of an object or a direction. The context slightly changes the meaning: sometimes it is really "the other side" (an opposite bank), sometimes it is simply "a side" or "a direction." What remains constant is the idea of being beyond a line or a boundary.
H5676H.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that God's promises concerned a land to be conquered, to be crossed to possess — it was not immediately where the Israelites were. It invites reflection on the biblical idea of passage, transition, and how God leads His people from one side to the other. It is also a word that anchors the Bible in real geography, that of the Jordan and Canaan.

sens: The bank or region that lies on the other side of a natural boundary, especially of a river
What is located opposite, on the opposite slope
The space that extends beyond, in the direction of a landmark
H5676I.detail:
1. The word first designates a geographical region separated by a natural barrier. In 1 Kings 4:24, it refers to the territories placed "on the other side of the river" — those extending beyond the Euphrates, under the control of the king. It is a region defined by its position relative to a reference point: the bank of a watercourse.
2. More broadly, it refers to anything that is on the opposite side, on the opposite face of a place or boundary. The word captures the idea of separation: there is an here and a beyond, two distinct spaces.
3. In Hebrew thought, the expression "on the other side of the river" carries particular weight: it designates distant lands, border areas that mark the limits of the controlled territory.
H5676I.origine: The Hebrew word עֵבֶר (ever) comes from a root that expresses the idea of crossing or passing from one side to the other. Its fundamental meaning is spatial: it is what is "on the other side" of a separation. In biblical context, the term is regularly used for regions located beyond a river or a natural boundary, particularly the Euphrates, which was a major geopolitical limit of the ancient Near East.
H5676I.emploi: The word appears once in the French Old Testament as "other side." In 1 Kings 4:24, it qualifies the extent of King Solomon's power: his dominion extends over the regions "on the other side of the river," that is, beyond the Euphrates. It is an administrative and geopolitical term, used to define the borders of a territory or sphere of influence. Its usage emphasizes the vastness of the controlled lands: the king reigns not only in Israel but also over the distant lands located beyond the rivers.
H5676I.portee: This word reminds us how the ancient Israelites conceived of space and delineated the borders of their world. Reading that the king dominates the regions "on the other side of the river," one grasps the immensity of the promised territory and the power of a kingship at its peak. It also highlights how natural rivers marked the limits of the known and the controlled.

sens: Patriarchal ancestor, son of Shelah and father of Peleg and Joktan
Old Testament figure belonging to the genealogy of Shem
H5677G.detail: 1. Heber is a man living in the time of the Patriarchs, mentioned for the first time in Genesis 10:21. He is the son of Shelah and the father of Peleg and Joktan (Genesis 10:24-25). His existence is also reported in the genealogy of Genesis 11, where it is learned that he fathered Peleg at the age of thirty-four (Genesis 11:16). Heber belongs to the lineage of Shem, one of the three sons of Noah, and he represents an important link in the genealogical chain that connects the origins of humanity to the fathers of the people of God.
H5677G.origine: The name Heber (עֵבֶר in Hebrew) literally means "the region beyond" or "one who is beyond." This meaning evokes the idea of crossing or passage to a distant territory. The name carries the image of a limit or boundary, perhaps suggesting distance or the crossing of lands. In the biblical genealogy, Heber represents a pivotal generation, as it is from his time that the division of the land is said to have occurred according to the Bible, a significant event reported by his son Peleg.
H5677G.emploi: Heber appears eleven times in the Bible, primarily in the genealogies of Genesis and Chronicles. In Genesis 10 and 11, he is presented as a link in the direct genealogical chain descending from Noah through Shem. His genealogical importance is underscored by the fact that he begets Peleg, whose name recalls the division (peleg) of the lands that took place in his time. The Bible also mentions his other son, Joktan (Genesis 10:25). Heber is also cited in Numbers 24:24 and in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles. The text highlights the longevity of Heber and his descendants, a characteristic of the antediluvian patriarchs and the period following the flood.
H5677G.portee: Heber embodies the continuity of God's plan through the generations. His inscription in the biblical genealogy reminds us that God preserves a faithful lineage throughout history, from Noah to the patriarchs and beyond. For the believer, Heber is a testimony to the patience and faithfulness of God toward His creation, even in ancient times when few names are known to us. The context of the land division under his son Peleg also illustrates how major events in human history fit into God's design.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H5677H.detail: 1. Eber is a family chief of the tribe of Gad, mentioned only once in the Bible as one of the seven brothers, sons of Abihail (1 Chronicles 5:13). These brothers formed an important lineage among the Gadites, and Eber is listed alongside Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jaecan, and Zia.
H5677H.origine: The name Eber literally means "the region beyond" or "one who comes from beyond." In the Old Testament, this name has been borne by several different people: the great-grandson of Shem and ancestor of the peoples speaking languages close to Hebrew (from which the Hebrews descend), several Israelite chiefs from different tribes, and a priest during the time of Jehoiakim. The meaning of the name may evoke a distant origin or passage, in accordance with its etymological significance.
H5677H.emploi: Eber appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, within a genealogical list of the descendants of Gad. He is presented as one of the seven sons of Abihail, all heads of paternal houses within the tribe. This mention is part of the genealogical records of Gad, which enumerated the most important families of this tribe established east of the Jordan.

sens: Son of Elpaal, of the tribe of Benjamin
H5677I.detail: Eber is a Benjamite, son of Elpaal and grandson of Sharahaim. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:12, where the genealogy of Benjamin lists his children. He is the brother of Mischeam (or Misham) and Shemer (or Shemed), among others.
H5677I.origine: The name Eber literally means "the region beyond" or "one who crosses." It is a name borne by several characters in the Bible, including the antediluvian ancestor Eber son of Salah, but also by other individuals, notably Benjamites and Gadites.
H5677I.emploi: Eber appears only once in the provided biblical usages: in 1 Chronicles 8:12, where he is presented as a son of Elpaal and an ancestor in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. This mention is part of a genealogical list establishing the lineages of Benjamin at the time of the divided monarchy. The context shows that Eber was an important figure of his generation, as he is listed among the sons of Elpaal.

sens: Benjamite mentioned only once in the biblical genealogies
H5677J.detail: Eber is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, living at the time of the division of the monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Shashak and the brother of several other sons of this same family (Ishpan, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel), as indicated in the genealogical list of 1 Chronicles 8:22.
H5677J.origine: The name Eber (or Heber in Hebrew עֵבֶר) literally means "the region beyond" or "that which is beyond." This name was borne by several important characters in biblical history: notably a descendant of Shem, father of Peleg and Joktan, who gave his name to the Hebrews, as well as by a Gadite chief. Here, it refers to a simple member of the Benjamite genealogy, with no apparent connection to these more famous namesakes.
H5677J.emploi: Eber appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:22, in a detailed genealogical list of the descendants of Sharahaim among the Benjamites. He is cited among the sons of Shashak, with no further details about his life or role. This unique mention places him in the category of minor characters whose memory is preserved in genealogies without reporting particular events.

sens: Priest during the time of Jehoiakim
H5677K.detail: Eber is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile: he is cited among the heads of priestly families at the time of Jehoiakim, son of Joshua (Nehemiah 12:20). His name appears in the list of priests who returned from Babylon to restore worship at the temple in Jerusalem.
H5677K.origine: The name Eber literally means "the region beyond" or "one who passes beyond." It is a Hebrew name borne by several important characters in the Bible: notably a great-grandson of Shem, ancestor of many nations, and several other men of Israel. In this passage, it simply designates a priest during the restoration of the temple.
H5677K.emploi: Eber appears only once in the Bible: in Nehemiah 12:20, where he is named as one of the heads of priestly families at the time of the high priest Jehoiakim, son of Joshua. This context is that of the return from exile to Jerusalem, when the Jewish people strive to rebuild the temple and restore worship. His inclusion in this official list shows his role as a religious leader in the restored community.

sens: Violent overflow of anger, irresistible outburst
Unleashed divine anger, terrible punishment
Arrogance, haughty pride, contempt
Flow or torrent (concrete sense)
H5678.detail:
1. Fury is primarily an overflow: like a liquid that explodes out of its container, it is an anger so violent that it cannot be contained. In Genesis 49:7, Jacob curses the anger of Simeon and Levi because it is "violent," unrestrained; it is a rage that destroys everything in its path.
2. In the Bible, fury often takes the form of God's anger in response to sin. In Ezekiel 22:21, God announces that He will blow "with the fire of My fury" — the image of consuming fire shows how this anger becomes a terrible and destructive judgment, purifying by destroying.
3. The word also means arrogance or haughty pride. In Jeremiah 48:30, God says He knows the "presumption" of the Moabites: it is this excessive pride that leads one to believe they can defy God, which in turn attracts this divine fury.
4. Rarely, the word retains a concrete sense: it designates an overflow or physical flood, like the foam of a wave or a flood.
H5678.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to overflow, to exceed." This is why it evokes the idea of something going beyond its limits: an anger that overflows out of control, an arrogance that surpasses boundaries. The fundamental meaning is excess, surpassing.
H5678.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea) and in the Psalms and Proverbs. It generally describes God's anger against injustice or idolatry: in Isaiah 13:9, the "day of the Lord" is characterized by anger and fury that will "exterminate sinners." The word can also refer to the arrogance of men who oppose God (Jeremiah 48:30; Amos 1:11), or even the unjust and destructive anger of humans against one another (Genesis 49:7). It nuances the expression "anger" by adding the idea of overflowing and irrepressible violence.
H5678.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's anger is never capricious, but a just reaction to evil. It also teaches that one's own pride and rage, if not submitted to God, only multiply destruction. Finally, it shows that God's mercy (which "withdraws His fury" according to Psalms 85:4) is a tremendous grace, for we deserve His judgment.

sens: Vessel used to cross a body of water
Means of transport to pass from one bank to another
H5679.detail:
1. The word designates a boat designed to cross a river or stream. It is a small ferry, a kind of raft or sturdy boat, intended to carry people and goods from one bank to the other. In 2 Samuel 19:18, this boat was crossing the Jordan to transport the household of King David during his return to Jerusalem: it was therefore a service vessel, practical and reliable.
2. By extension, the word can also refer to the action of crossing itself, the passage of a body of water. But in the Bible, it mainly appears as the object that makes this passage possible — the concrete means to cross a natural boundary.
H5679.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to pass" or "to cross." It is built on the same root as verbs and nouns related to the idea of passage and crossing. The image is that of crossing a body of water, and the ferry boat is literally what allows one to "pass over" the waters.
H5679.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 19:18. It is a technical term to designate a specific type of boat — not a large sea vessel, but a river crossing ferry. The context is that of King David's return after a rebellion, and this boat was used to transport his court and goods across the Jordan, a river that constituted a major barrier in the land of Israel.
H5679.portee: This passage reminds us that even natural obstacles like rivers cannot prevent God's plan from being fulfilled. David's return, facilitated by simple means (a crossing boat), shows the divine Providence that provides His king with the resources to return to Jerusalem and to his throne.

sens: Descendant of Eber, member of the people of Israel
Israelite, particularly in the context of relations with foreign nations
The language spoken by the Hebrews
H5680.detail:
1. The term "Hebrew" primarily designates a member of the people descended from Eber, ancestor of the patriarchs. It is a name of people and lineage. Abram is called "the Hebrew" in Genesis 14:13, which situates him in his ancestral and ethnic identity.
2. In passages where Hebrews interact with foreigners — Egyptians, Philistines, or other nations — the word takes on the color of a distinct, recognizable, and separable identity. In Genesis 43:32, the Egyptians cannot eat with the Hebrews because it is "an abomination" in their eyes; in Exodus 3:18, Moses must go tell Pharaoh that "the Lord, the God of the Hebrews" has sent him. The word then marks the difference, the otherness.
3. The word can also refer to the Hebrew language itself, the idiom spoken by this people.
H5680.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "to pass, to cross" — the image is that of one who comes "from the other side," "from beyond." The Hebrews are the descendants of Eber, whose name carries this same idea of "beyond." It is a word that, in a way, preserves the memory of a people who have traveled, who come from elsewhere.
H5680.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis and Exodus, and also in 1 Samuel and Jeremiah. It is typical of narratives where Hebrews confront other peoples: Abram in Canaan surrounded by Amorites (Genesis 14:13), Moses before Pharaoh (Exodus 3:18, 9:13), the Hebrew slaves in Egypt (Exodus 1-2), the Hebrews facing the Philistines (1 Samuel 13-14). The context is often one of asserting identity, maintaining separation, or conquering freedom. In Jeremiah 34:9 and 14, the word designates the Hebrew slave to whom the Law of Moses grants special rights: it is a legal and religious category apart.
H5680.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the people of Israel has a unique identity and history willed by God. It is the people through whom God chose to reveal Himself and act. Recognizing the Hebrews is to acknowledge the concrete rooting of the Christian faith in a human history, that of the people of Israel, and not in an abstraction.

sens: Chief of a Levitical family during the time of King David
H5681.detail: 1. Ibri was a Levite from the family of Merari, belonging to the branch of the descendants of Jaaziah. He is mentioned in the register of Levitical house leaders established during the time of King David, alongside his brothers Schoham and Zaccur (1 Chronicles 24:27).
H5681.origine: The name Ibri literally means "Hebrew" in Hebrew. It is a rare name in the Bible, borne here by a member of the tribe of Levi responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple. His appearance in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles shows the importance given to documenting priestly families.
H5681.emploi: Ibri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:27. He is listed among the Levitical house leaders during the time of King David, in the register of the divisions of the Levites. His brief mention indicates that he held a role in the organization of temple worship, as a member of the family of Merari.

sens: Mountain range east of the Jordan, in the land of Moab, facing Jericho
Place where Moses viewed the promised land before dying
Landmark for Israel's routes in the desert
H5682.detail:
1. Abarim is a mountain range located east of the Jordan, in the region of Moab, facing the city of Jericho. Mount Nebo is part of it. It is a series of rocky peaks that overlooks the surrounding plains and marks the eastern border of the territory that God is about to give to Israel (Numbers 27:12).

2. This place becomes famous in biblical history as the last starting point for Moses. At the end of his days, God commands the prophet to go up these mountains — specifically to Mount Nebo — to view the land of Canaan from afar, a promise he will never conquer himself (Deuteronomy 32:49).

3. The mountains of Abarim also appear as a stop in the account of Israel's wanderings in the desert. The people camp at Almon-Diblathaim, then at the mountains of Abarim, and finally in the plains of Moab by the Jordan (Numbers 33:47-48). It is a major geographical landmark for locating the journey.
H5682.origine: The name Abarim literally means "regions beyond" or "passages": it refers to the lands located beyond the Jordan, a transitional area. In Hebrew, the word evokes the idea of crossing a boundary, going to the other side. Mount Nebo, which is part of it, itself bears the name of a mountain of passage and revelation.
H5682.emploi: Abarim appears five times in the Bible, always referring to the same mountain range. Three occurrences are found in the Pentateuch (Numbers and Deuteronomy), at the time when Israel completes its desert journey and camps facing Canaan. Twice (Numbers 27:12 and Deuteronomy 32:49), God commands Moses to go up these mountains, leading to the account of his death and the burial of the prophet. Once, Jeremiah refers to Abarim poetically, as a high place from which one cries out (Jeremiah 22:20). The name remains associated with the divine boundary between the desert of the Exodus and the Promised Land.
H5682.portee: For the Christian reader, Abarim symbolizes a threshold: the point where one stage ends and another begins. It is on these mountains that Moses, after forty years of faithfulness, sees the promise fulfilled without entering it — an image of faith that accepts what God accomplishes beyond what we experience. It is also a place from which one contemplates the distant horizon, a reminder that true victory belongs to God alone.

sens: City of the tribe of Asher in northern Galilee
H5683.detail: Ébron is a city mentioned in the division of the lands of Canaan, assigned to the tribe of Asher. It is located in northern Galilee, near Sidon (Joshua 19:28). It is another name for the city of Abdon.
H5683.origine: The name Ébron means "alliance" in Hebrew. It comes from the root that denotes the bond, the commitment between two parties. This name reflects the spiritual importance of alliances in the history of Israel.
H5683.emploi: Ébron appears only once in the Bible (Joshua 19:28), during the description of the borders and cities assigned to the tribe of Asher after the conquest of Canaan. It is also known by the name Abdon. This city was part of the northern region of Canaan, not far from the Phoenician territory of Sidon.

sens: Camping station of the Israelites in the desert
H5684.detail: Abrona is a station where the Israelites stopped and set up camp during their wandering in the desert, just before arriving at Etsjon-Gueber (Numbers 33:34-35). It appears in the list of stops on the journey from Egypt to the Promised Land, marking a resting point for the people during forty years of travel.
H5684.origine: The name Abrona literally means "passage" in Hebrew, evoking a place of transition or a spot where one crosses. This name reflects the very nature of these desert stations: temporary waypoints on the path to the divine promise.
H5684.emploi: Abrona appears only twice in the Bible, in chapter 33 of Numbers, which systematically lists the forty-two stops of the Israelites' journey from their departure from Egypt. It is mentioned after Jothbatha and before Etsjon-Gueber, thus situating its precise place in the desert itinerary. It is an element of the historical framework of the Exodus, in this administrative and memorial document of the people.

sens: To dry up, lose moisture (referring to seeds or plants)
To gradually consume, wither away
H5685.detail:
1. The word refers to the process by which a seed or plant loses its water and dries up. In Joel 1:17, the seeds "dry up" under the clods of earth due to drought or the plague of locusts: they cannot germinate, they die on the spot.
2. In a broader sense, the word evokes anything that consumes and weakens gradually, like an organism that withers. The image is one of slow destruction due to lack of vital moisture.
H5685.origine: The Hebrew verb עָבַשׁ (avash) literally means "to dry up" or "to shrivel." It likely comes from a root that expresses the idea of contraction and drying. The word belongs to a small group of Hebrew verbs describing the destruction of vegetation by natural causes (drought, heat) or by God's judgment.
H5685.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Joel 1:17. The context is one of agricultural catastrophe: the region is experiencing a terrible drought or a locust invasion, and all vegetation dies. The seeds dry up before they can even germinate. This word fits into the dramatic picture of God's judgment on the land, where all plant life disappears, leading to famine and economic ruin.
H5685.portee: This word reminds us of the fragility of creation and the importance of water for life. For the biblical reader, it illustrates how natural disasters, seen as manifestations of divine judgment, destroy all hope: the seeds that cannot germinate symbolize death and the absence of a future. It is an invitation to recognize God as the master of life and death.

sens: To weave together, intertwine threads
To unite efforts, act in concert
To conspire, collude in agreement
H5686.detail:
1. In a literal and concrete sense, the word means to intertwine or weave together several threads to make a single fabric: one crosses and ties the strands to unite them securely.
2. The text of Micah uses it in a figurative sense: to make common cause means to unite one's efforts with others for a common purpose, to act together, in concert. Here, the prince, the judge, and the prominent figure unite in a common conspiracy to commit evil and exploit the people (Micah 7:3).
3. The expression then evokes a secret alliance or collusion: several powerful individuals bind together, like woven threads, to pursue a shared goal, often dishonest or unjust.
H5686.origine: The Hebrew verb עָבַת (avat) comes from a root that primarily means "to weave" or "to intertwine": it evokes the concrete image of fingers crossing and tying threads on a loom. This image of interwoven weaving has naturally extended to the figurative sense of uniting, binding together, and then uniting for a common action.
H5686.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Micah 7:3. The context is one of prophetic denunciation: the prophet describes the moral corruption of his time, where all the powerful — prince, judge, great — conspire together, making common cause to exploit the people. The image of weaving reinforces the idea that they are linked, intertwined in a common fabric of malice.
H5686.portee: This word reminds us that there is a solidarity of evil: the powerful who act unjustly and without fear of God bind together to form a system of oppression. The Christian reading this passage sees a warning: those who reject God and His justice can very well unite in evil. But there is also comfort: the prophet speaks, God sees, and His word of judgment will be fulfilled. The Christian must never make common cause with evil, even if everything around him conspires to seduce him.

sens: Having dense foliage, rich in branches and leaves
Providing thick and protective shade
Serving as a refuge or gathering place
H5687.detail:
1. The word describes a tree whose branches and leaves are tightly packed, forming a compact and green mass. This is the visible aspect of abundant and well-developed vegetation. In Leviticus 23:40, the Israelites are to gather "branches of dense trees" to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles, recognizable by their thick foliage.
2. A dense tree naturally creates a thick shade under which one can rest or hide. This quality makes it valuable in a hot and sunny climate. Ezekiel 6:13 mentions idolatrous rites that took place "under every green tree, under every dense oak," secluded places where the thick foliage provided intimacy.
3. By extension, a dense tree becomes a symbolic place of refuge or meeting. The passages in Ezekiel suggest that these dense trees, visible from afar on the hills, attracted people for their religious practices — whether legitimate (Feast of Tabernacles) or idolatrous (illegitimate cults).
H5687.origine: The Hebrew word עָבוֹת (avot) comes from a root related to the idea of "weaving" or "interlacing." The foliage of a dense tree indeed resembles intertwined branches, forming a dense and compact whole. The same root can express the idea of thickness and density, which perfectly corresponds to the description of rich and tight vegetation.
H5687.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in botanical contexts. In Leviticus 23:40 and Nehemiah 8:15, it designates the leafy branches to be gathered for the festive rites of the Feast of Tabernacles — identifiable by their abundant foliage. In Ezekiel 6:13 and 20:28, the context is more critical: the dense trees are the places where Israel offered sacrifices to idols, taking advantage of the shade and isolation that their thick foliage provided. The meaning remains constant: it is always about the visible density of the foliage, but the moral use varies depending on whether the presence of dense trees aids in legitimate or illegitimate worship.
H5687.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God recognizes and approves certain places and acts of celebration — such as the Feast of Tabernacles with its green branches. Conversely, Ezekiel shows how the shade and intimacy provided by "dense trees" can become complicit in idolatry: what is beautiful in itself becomes perverse when diverted from the true God. It is an invitation to examine our places of gathering and our religious practices — are they dedicated to the honor of the living God?

sens: Braided or coiled object used to bind, hold, or attach
Chain or link that restrains, imprisons, or enslaves
Thick and intertwined branch of a tree
H5688.detail:
1. A cord is an object made by braiding or coiling threads or strands, intended to bind, hold, or suspend something. It is a material, concrete object common in daily life. In biblical times, it was notably used for the ornamentation of the priestly garment: the ephod is adorned with braided cords of fine gold (Exodus 28:14).
2. In a figurative sense, the cord represents a link that enchains or enslaves — a restraint on freedom. The Psalms speak of breaking the chains that bind us (Psalms 2:3), and the prophet Isaiah denounces those who willingly attach themselves to sin as if they were dragging themselves with cords (Isaiah 5:18).
3. The cord also refers to the thick and intertwined branches that provide the strength of a mighty tree — an image of strength and branching. Ezekiel uses this meaning when he speaks of the vigorous branches of a great cedar (Ezekiel 31:3).
H5688.origine: The Hebrew word עֲבֹת comes from a root expressing the idea of braiding, of turning together. It primarily designates the manufactured object obtained by this braiding: a cord. The same word naturally applies to the branches that intertwine in a tree, as they suggest a natural braiding. In a metaphorical context, what binds or restrains is also called a cord — hence the use of the word for chains representing moral or political enslavement.
H5688.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, first in descriptions of the equipment of the tabernacle: the golden cords of the priestly ephod (Exodus 28:14, 28:25, 39:18). It is found in the story of Samson, where cords attempt to hold him prisoner (Judges 16:11-12). In biblical poetry and prophecy, the word takes on a metaphorical significance: the psalms and prophets use it to describe the ties of evil, sin, or political enslavement (Psalms 2:3, Isaiah 5:18). Ezekiel uses it for the thick branches of trees symbolizing power (Ezekiel 31:3).
H5688.portee: The cord reminds the believer that sin and evil are ties that hinder true freedom. It invites us to recognize how we voluntarily attach ourselves to passions and lies. Conversely, it speaks of solidity and strength when used rightly — hence the biblical call to break the chains of evil and find freedom in God.

sens: to experience intense carnal passion, a burning desire for someone
to be obsessively attracted to a person, to the point of losing discernment
to be seduced and dominated by carnal lust
H5689.detail:
1. The verb first describes an inflaming of desire: it is an inner heat, a passion that burns and consumes. In Ezekiel 23:5, Oholah "was inflamed" for the Assyrians, showing that this desire seized and possessed her.
2. This desire is never neutral: it leads to a loss of judgment and shameful acts. Ezekiel 23:7 shows how she who "was inflamed" for her lovers became "defiled" with them, revealing that this fire of desire leads to impurity and unfaithfulness.
3. The word also designates the objects of this desire: in Jeremiah 4:30, the "lovers" are those for whom one is inflamed, these men who exploit the passion one has for them without respect or true love.
H5689.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of burning, of heating intensely. The metaphor of fire for carnal desire is universal: desire burns like a flame. The verb in Hebrew is simple and vigorous, unambiguous about the physical and impulsive nature of this passion.
H5689.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the Bible, primarily in Ezekiel 23, where it describes the unfaithfulness of Jerusalem (figuratively represented as Oholah) toward the Lord. Six times it is translated as "was inflamed": it is the expression of a passion that consumes and misleads. Only once (Jeremiah 4:30) is the participle translated as "lovers" to designate the men who are the object of this desire. All uses carry a clearly negative moral connotation: the burning desire is presented as unfaithfulness to God and as the cause of inner defilement.
H5689.portee: This word invites the reader to examine the nature of their affections and desires. The Bible does not hide that carnal desire is a powerful force, but it calls us not to be consumed by it. The contrast between Jerusalem, who "is inflamed" for lovers who despise her, and the call to faithfulness to God teaches that true security and dignity are found in a right relationship with the Lord, not in submission to passions that enslave us.

sens: Fleshly desire or passion of the senses, attraction to bodily pleasures
Carnal desire, greed related to physical or sensual appetites
Inclination of the heart towards material or carnal enjoyments
H5690.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes an intense physical attraction, a raw desire of the senses — the call of the body rather than the spirit. In Ezekiel 33:31, the heart of the people "gives itself to greed": their thoughts and desires are directed towards pleasures, not towards God and His words.

2. More broadly, it expresses a visceral lust, the inclination of the heart towards what flatters the senses or satisfies appetite — wealth, pleasure, luxury. It is not a pious admiration, but a carnal and selfish desire. The people listen to Ezekiel as one listens to a beautiful singer (v. 32), for auditory pleasure, without wanting to convert.
H5690.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of carnal desire and sensual greed. It stands in opposition to spiritual desire, the wish to know and obey God. The context of Ezekiel shows that this word paints a heart turned away from God, attached to the immediate pleasures of the flesh and the senses.
H5690.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both passages in Ezekiel chapter 33. In Ezekiel 33:31, translators render the word as "mockery" (the people treat the prophet's words lightly), but the deeper meaning is greed: they listen without obeying because their hearts chase after other desires. In Ezekiel 33:32, the musical context ("singer" with a "beautiful voice") reinforces the idea: the people are seduced by aesthetic and carnal pleasure, not by the spiritual message. These two verses depict the same problem: a people whose hearts are tied to sensual appetites, closed to conversion.
H5690.portee: This word challenges the believer: are we listening to God with all our heart, or is our attention captured by the pleasures and desires of the moment? Ezekiel reminds us that true listening requires a heart freed from the bondage to carnal appetites, a sincere desire to obey, not mere aesthetic pleasure. It is a call to examine our true motives in our relationship with God.

sens: Intense carnal desire, unrestrained sexual attraction
Luxurious greed, unregulated appetite
H5691.detail:
1. The word denotes an intense carnal desire, a sexual attraction that escapes all moral control. It is the image of an appetite that carries the person away and pushes them towards what is forbidden. In Ezekiel 23:11, Oholiba is "more unrestrained than she in her passion" — she surpasses her sister in debauchery and in the frenzied pursuit of illegitimate relationships.
2. More broadly, it is luxurious greed, a state where the flesh dominates reason and desires become masters. The text makes it a symptom of grave infidelity: Oholiba "was more unrestrained" and "Her prostitutions exceeded those of her sister," showing how this passion drives her further into sin.
H5691.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of greed and carnal desire. It belongs to the biblical vocabulary of the flesh (basar) and its disordered appetites, often contrasted with self-control and obedience to divine Law. It is a rare word in the Old Testament, used mainly to describe serious disorders.
H5691.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 23:11. It is found in the chapter where the prophet describes the two sisters Oholah (Samaria) and Oholiba (Jerusalem) as unfaithful women: they represent the kingdoms of Israel and Judah that have turned away from God to seek alliances with other nations. Oholiba's passion is not only carnal; it is the symbol of spiritual infidelity, of political and religious greed that drives a people to apostasy.
H5691.portee: This word reminds the believer that disordered passions are a form of rupture with God. Unrestrained carnal passion leads to spiritual infidelity — this is what Scripture calls living according to the flesh rather than according to the Spirit. Ezekiel invites each one to examine their own desires and to seek self-control in God rather than being dominated by their appetites.

sens: Flat, round bread, baked on heated stones or in a hearth
Individual portion of cooked dough, often consumed quickly
Basic, simple, nourishing food, prepared in haste or on a journey
H5692.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes a flat, circular bread, baked on heated stones rather than in an oven: it is a simple and ancient technique, common in the Middle East. In 1 Kings 19:6, the prophet Elijah finds a cake baked on heated stones, ready to eat. 2. It is an individual portion of dough, smaller than a whole loaf: the widow of Zarephath prepares one for Elijah first (1 Kings 17:13), then makes others for herself and her son. 3. It is a simple and practical food, prepared quickly in case of need or while traveling: the Hebrews made it with unleavened dough during the flight from Egypt (Exodus 12:39), and the people made it in the desert with manna (Numbers 11:8).
H5692.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of forming in a circle or disk. It specifically denotes this flat, round shape, well-suited for cooking on stones. The Greek term that often translates it in ancient versions also evokes this individual and portable cake.
H5692.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It describes a daily food, prepared in ordinary (Genesis 18:6 during Abraham's visit) or extraordinary situations (the exodus from Egypt, the desert). The context always shows a simple food, most often unleavened, cooked quickly. Ezekiel 4:12 even mentions a cake of barley baked in an impure manner, symbolizing the calamity coming upon Jerusalem.
H5692.portee: This word reminds us that biblical faith does not overlook the concrete details of life: food, daily gestures, hospitality. It also shows how God provides for our simple needs — Elijah receives food when he is weary, the widow finds enough to live on. These ordinary cakes are the bread of providence.

sens: Migratory bird with a characteristic call, known for its regular migrations
Action of flying by lightly flapping the wings
Figuratively: lament or cry of distress
H5693.detail:
1. A crane is a well-known migratory bird in the East, returning each year at the same season. In Jeremiah 8:7, the bird is mentioned alongside the stork, the turtledove, and the swallow as an example of an animal that "knows its season in the heavens" — it arrives and departs regularly, unlike Israel which ignores "the law of the Lord." 
2. The word can also refer to the light action of flying by flapping the wings, as shown in Isaiah 38:14 where the sick man "flies" like a swallow (the translation "to flutter" conveys this movement), a gesture of worry and weakness.
3. By extension, the word takes on an emotional color: the cry or lament of the sick person who "flies" and "groans" in their suffering — it is the bird that cries, not out of joy, but out of distress or illness.
H5693.origine: The Hebrew word עָגוּר (agur) primarily denotes the migratory bird. Its basic image is that of a winged being that departs and returns, often associated with the cry. Biblical names of birds generally refer to a visible trait: the cry, the flight, or seasonal behavior. Here, it is the regular alternation and the gesture of flight that dominate.
H5693.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 38:14, the sick king (Hezekiah) compares himself to a creature that flies and cries under suffering. In Jeremiah 8:7, the bird becomes a silent reproach: it knows its time, but Israel does not know God's time. In both cases, it is the animal's natural instinct (faithful migration, cry of distress) that contrasts with human infidelity or weakness. The context is always one of reproach or lament.
H5693.portee: The crane reminds us that every creature obeys God's order with faithfulness: it arrives on time, it cries its instinct. In the face of this regularity, the people of God who transgress His law, or the believer in distress who can only cry, measures their distance from the created harmony. The bird thus becomes a silent call to return to God's ways.

sens: Circular or drop-shaped jewelry that is suspended from the ear
Personal ornament of value, often made of gold or precious metal
Mark of wealth or social rank
H5694.detail:
1. An earring is a piece of jewelry worn suspended from the ear, typically round or elongated in shape. It is an adornment that both men and women could wear in antiquity. In Numbers 31:50, the Israelites bring as an offering to God earrings found among the spoils of war, alongside other jewelry such as chains and necklaces.
2. The earring is a valuable ornament, often crafted from gold or precious metal. It signifies the wealth of the wearer. In Ezekiel 16:12, in the vision of Jerusalem as a adorned bride, God places earrings on the city's ears as a sign of beauty and dignity.
3. Wearing earrings indicated a certain social status or belonging to a group. It was an accessory favored by both wealthy men and women, symbolizing their position in society.
H5694.origine: The Hebrew word agîl comes from a root expressing the idea of turning or forming in a circle, hence the image of a round or suspended object. The circular shape or suspension is the essence of the jewelry. This term specifically refers to earrings or hoops, distinct from other types of jewelry such as bracelets or necklaces.
H5694.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the plural to denote earrings. In Numbers 31:50, it refers to the spoils of war consisting of precious jewelry that the Israelites dedicate to the Lord. In Ezekiel 16:12, in a symbolic vision, the earrings are among the ornaments that God places on Jerusalem, an image of beauty and covenant. In both cases, the jewelry embodies material wealth or splendor.
H5694.portee: The earring reminds us that visible wealth can be offered to God or used for His glory. In Ezekiel, it symbolizes how God adorns His people with beauty and dignity. These images invite the reader to reflect on the place of wealth in the life of faith and on the beauty that God grants to His people.

sens: Young bovine, domesticated farm animal
Animal sacrificed as an offering to God
Melted metal idol worshiped in place of the true God
Leg or foot compared to a calf's leg
H5695.detail:
1. The calf is a young bull, an animal raised for meat, milk, and labor. It is a common creature in the pastoral and agricultural world of the ancient Near East (Jeremiah 31:18 speaks of the people as a calf being trained).
2. In Israel's worship, calves were often offered as sacrifices or burnt offerings, valuable animals by their worth (Leviticus 9:2 and 9:3 describe calves offered to the Lord as sacrifices).
3. The calf becomes an idol when Israel makes statues of calves cast in gold or silver to worship in place of the Lord: the golden calf at Sinai is the most serious example (Exodus 32:4), later imitated by the northern kingdoms of Israel (2 Kings 17:16). These calves represent a major unfaithfulness, a return to the gods of the pagan nations.
4. The image of the calf is also used to describe body parts: the legs of a creature in a vision may appear like calves' legs (Ezekiel 1:7).
H5695.origine: The Hebrew word éguel comes from a root that evokes the agility and liveliness of the young animal — the root also suggests the idea of turning or moving. It is a young and vigorous animal, hence its use for valuable sacrifices. The word belongs to the vocabulary of ancient husbandry and pastoralism.
H5695.emploi: The word calf appears 35 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in two contexts. First, legal sacrifices and offerings: calves offered to the Lord in the tabernacle and the Temple, top-quality animals to honor God (Leviticus 9). Second, idolatry: the golden calf forged by Aaron at Sinai remains the foundational sin (Exodus 32), recalled in the Psalms (Psalms 106:19) and denounced by the prophets. The northern kingdom of Israel recreates this transgression by establishing calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28-29; 2 Kings 17:16). Other passages use the calf in a concrete sense: a farm animal slaughtered for a meal (1 Samuel 28:24), or as a poetic comparison in visions (Ezekiel 1:7).
H5695.portee: The calf in the Bible teaches the tension between the pure and the impure, true worship and idolatry. The golden calf reveals how easy it is to abandon the visible God and create gods in our image — a constant temptation for the human heart. But the sacrificed calf also reminds us that God accepts the offerings of the people when they come from a sincere heart. This duality invites the believer to examine their own hidden worship.

sens: In circular or curved shape
Having a surface or contour without angles
Constituting the upper or top part of an object
Being rounded, smoothed in its shapes
H5696.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a circular geometric shape: the great bronze "sea" of the Temple had a completely round shape, with ten cubits in diameter (1 Kings 7:23).
2. It also applies to circular openings: the opening at the base of the basin was round, as for works of this type (1 Kings 7:31).
3. The word can designate the highest or upper part of a structure: the upper part of the royal throne was rounded at the back (1 Kings 10:19), giving the whole a majestic appearance.
4. It also evokes a smoothed contour without angles: unlike square panels, some elements were rounded rather than geometrically precise (1 Kings 7:31).
H5696.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of circular, curved, or coiled. It belongs to the vocabulary of shape and geometry. In Hebrew, this word translates the simple observation of a natural or crafted shape that follows a curved line rather than an angular one. The root is related to the idea of rotation or circumference.
H5696.emploi: The word appears five times in the Bible, exclusively in architectural descriptions of the Temple of Jerusalem and the royal palace. It primarily qualifies the great bronze sea, this monumental basin used by the priests for their washings (1 Kings 7:23 and its parallel in 2 Chronicles 4:2). It is also used for the openings and upper parts of the Temple furniture, where the round shape confers elegance and perfection to the work. Its context is always that of sacred or royal architecture, emphasizing that divine perfection is also manifested in the harmony of forms.
H5696.portee: This word reminds us that beauty and harmony of forms matter in the worship rendered to God. The round bronze sea was not just a utilitarian basin: its perfect shape reflected the wisdom and glory of the Creator. The meticulous description of the proportions and shapes of the Temple teaches that God cares about the beauty of His earthly dwelling, inviting believers to honor God with excellence in their works and worship.

sens: young female cow
offering to the God of Israel
draft animal
H5697A.detail:
1. A heifer is a young female cow, before she has had a calf. It is a robust animal, suitable for agricultural work, but the text often specifies a heifer "that has not been used for work" (Deuteronomy 21:3), emphasizing its purity and inactivity.
2. In sacrifice and ritual, the heifer holds a particular role in Israelite worship. Abraham is commanded to take "a three-year-old heifer" for a solemn sacrifice (Genesis 15:9). Even more singularly, a flawless heifer, never yoked, must be slaughtered as a rite of atonement when a murder goes unpunished (Deuteronomy 21:4), where it becomes the object of a grave ritual act: the elders wash their hands over its body to signify their innocence.
3. Figuratively, the heifer is associated with the productive strength and prosperity of the people. Jeremiah calls Israel "a well-fed heifer" that rebels against God (Jeremiah 46:20), an image of pride and independence. In the riddle of Samson, "to plow with another's heifer" becomes an expression of intimacy or trust (Judges 14:18).
H5697A.origine: The Hebrew word עֶגְלָה (eglah) comes from a root that evokes the young animal, youth. The Greek ἐμός or related terms from the Septuagint regularly translate it with words specifically designating a young cow. It is a classical term in biblical Hebrew, used both in the north and south, and belongs to the ancient pastoral and sacrificial vocabulary.
H5697A.emploi: The word "heifer" appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the Old Testament. It is present in very different contexts: first sacrificial (Genesis 15:9, where Abraham offers a heifer in a theophany), then legal and ritual (Deuteronomy 21, where it serves as atonement for an unresolved murder). Outside of rituals, the word shifts to the figurative: Samson uses it to speak of a personal relationship (Judges 14:18), the prophets mention it to evoke the arrogance of Israel or its enemies (Jeremiah 46:20 and 50:11, where Babylon is depicted as a well-fed heifer that refuses its yoke; Hosea 10:11, where Israel is a trained heifer). The word thus retains its concrete rooting while opening up to symbolic uses.
H5697A.portee: The heifer reminds us that God accepts sacrifice, even offerings at the cost of shed blood, provided the heart is sincere. It also embodies a form of divine justice: in the rite of Deuteronomy 21, it represents the sacredness of human life and community solidarity in the face of crime. Its prophetic evocation invites the reader to recognize when they give in to pride or rebellion, like a rebellious beast that refuses the yoke of God's will.

sens: Geographical location near Zoar, south of Moab
H5697B.detail: 1. Eglatschelischija is a place mentioned in the prophecies against Moab. Its name literally means "the heifer of the third year," which may have been the name of a city or region known for cattle raising. This place was located near Zoar (the city where Lot fled during the destruction of Sodom) and in the southern region of Moab.
H5697B.origine: The name Eglatschelischija is composed of two Hebrew words: "egla" (heifer, young cow) and "schelischija" (third). In the Old Testament, animals of a certain age had symbolic value: this three-year-old heifer could evoke an animal at the peak of its strength, which may explain why a locality received this expressive name.
H5697B.emploi: Eglatschelischija appears only twice in the Bible, both times in prophecies of doom concerning Moab. Isaiah 15:5 and Jeremiah 48:34 mention this place as a geographical landmark in the cries of distress of the Moabite people in the face of divine judgment. These two prophecies use Eglatschelischija to precisely locate the regions affected by the catastrophe.

sens: Wife of David during the time of the united monarchy
H5698.detail: Eglah is one of David's wives, mentioned only in two genealogical lists (2 Samuel 3:5 and 1 Chronicles 3:3). She is the mother of Ithream, David's sixth son born in Hebron. The name literally means "heifer" in Hebrew, which evokes strength and fertility.
H5698.origine: The Hebrew name Eglah (עֶגְלָה) comes from the root that designates a young cow or heifer. This type of animal name was not rare in the ancient Near East: it could express an admired physical quality or a blessing. The contrast is striking: David, king of Israel, chooses wives from diverse origins and statuses, reflecting the political alliances and practices of his time.
H5698.emploi: Eglah appears only twice in the Bible, in royal lists of David's sons born in Hebron during his youth, before he became king over all Israel. These two passages (2 Samuel 3:5 and 1 Chronicles 3:3) are parallel and serve to document the royal genealogy. She is presented only as one of the royal mothers, with no additional details about her life or role.

sens: Wheeled vehicle pulled by animals (oxen, horses) for transporting people or goods
War chariot, military equipment equipped with wheels
Sacred chariot, vehicle used in a religious or cultic context
H5699.detail:
1. The chariot is primarily a simple utility vehicle, pulled by draft animals, used for moving or transporting things. When Jacob was aging in Egypt, Pharaoh sent chariots so that his family could join him comfortably (Genesis 46:5). It is the practical means of transport in the ancient world, regularly used by the wealthy and powerful.
2. The chariot also becomes a weapon of war: it is a light and fast military instrument, pulled by horses, from which arrows are launched or the enemy is charged. The psalms speak of the day when God will break the war chariots, putting an end to conflicts (Psalms 46:10). It is the most advanced and deadly technological equipment of ancient battles.
3. The chariot can also serve to transport sacred objects: the ark of the covenant was placed on a chariot to be brought back to Israel (1 Samuel 6:8), which shows the deep respect reserved for the things of God. It is both a practical means and an act of veneration.
H5699.origine: The Hebrew word agalah comes from a root that designates rolling or circular movement. It is related to Semitic words describing everything that turns or rolls. In Hebrew, the same root is found in other terms related to movement or wheels. It is a very ancient word, common to several languages of the Near East, because the chariot was a central element of ancient life, from transport to war.
H5699.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical narratives from the Exodus to the royal period. It designates sometimes a simple transport cart (Genesis 45-46, where Pharaoh sends chariots to welcome Jacob), sometimes a religious equipment (1 Samuel 6, where the chariot transports the ark), sometimes a war instrument (Psalms 46:10, where God breaks the chariots). It is also found in the lists of offerings for the tabernacle (Numbers 7), which shows the importance of this asset in the ancient economy. The context changes the weight of the word: it is an everyday object or a symbol of power depending on what is being recounted.
H5699.portee: Understanding the chariot helps the reader visualize the concrete life of the biblical world: it is the means of transport, the weapon, the tool of work of the ancients. It also sheds light on how the Bible measures wealth and power: to possess chariots was to be powerful. Finally, when God promises to break the chariots, He promises peace and the end of violence. This seemingly technical detail brings the reader into the real universe of the Bible and helps understand that God acts in the concrete history of men.
